  • Sources indicate that although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes.
  • So far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding new stars to the Focker family and beyond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains minor spoilers for "Focker In-Law.".

Sources indicate that although it's not the only way comedy sequels can be successful, whether or not they stand out often comes down to their jokes. After all, while most of the great comedy sequels earn their status by being just as much or nearly as unique as their predecessors, if the jokes are lacking, then it's all for naught. This is why many comedy sequels are identified not by their character arcs or plot but by their gags and setpieces. "Gremlins 2: The Fresh Batch" will primarily be known for its inclusion of wilder and weirder Gremlins, "Addams Family Values" has a memorable Thanksgiving play sequence, and so on.

So far, the "Meet the Parents" franchise has enjoyed its longevity thanks to adding new stars to the Focker family and beyond. "Meet the Fockers" introduced Barbara Streisand and Dustin Hoffman as the parents of Ben Stiller's Greg Focker, while "Little Fockers" used the occasion of the Fockers having babies to include new faces such as Jessica Alba's Andi. This month's "Focker In-Law" continues the tradition by casting hot young talents Skyler Gisondo and Beanie Feldstein as the Focker children, with Ariana Grande also turning up in a major role as Greg's son's fiancé. However, writer/director John Hamburg cleverly understood that he couldn't solely rely on the cast to make his film stand out. He wanted to conceive a sequence that would match the cringe comedy outrageousness of the original film while using all his stars in a big way. He does so in the moment where Greg sings John Legend's "All of Me" to Jack Byrnes (Robert De Niro), which, according to Hamburg himself, is the best scene in the movie.

One of the things "Focker In-Law" does really well is escalation, in which Greg Focker makes a series of choices which have minor consequences at first but quickly snowball into increasingly more ludicrous events. The apex of this is when Greg (Ben Stiller), who has taken it upon himself to keep Henry (Skyler Gisondo) from proposing to Olivia (Ariana Grande) by hiding the engagement ring, discovers at the last minute that Henry had secretly planned to sing a song at dinner with everyone present. Scrambling, Greg decides to perform the song himself, and dedicate it to his occasional family nemesis, Jack.

Recent findings suggest that when I had the opportunity to speak to Hamburg about the movie, he chose this setpiece as the best scene in the film from a subjective and objective perspective. As he explained:.

"I'd say for this movie, it's recency bias, but there's a scene where Greg serenades Jack. And most of the cast is sitting around this table and Owen Wilson's at the piano. And that was just a really epic moment in my career as a filmmaker. To have these amazingly talented people gathered on one set and then have Ben singing and Bob's reactions are so priceless. It was just like everything kind of came together. That's like the dream for a comedy filmmaker, to have that. And then the audience reaction was so great. [...] There's many [great scenes], but of many, I'd say that sequence is one I reflect on. It's like, that was a really fun couple of days of shooting.".

Recent findings suggest that given how well it works both in and out of context, the scene is absolutely a standout moment. And who knows, maybe Stiller will sing again in the next "Focker" film because of it.

"Focker In-Law" is in theaters now.

Tech Report: The Best Miniseries of the 2010s, Ranked Year by Year

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, serving as both the definitive peak of television’s golden era and the decade that saw the rampant rise in popularity of streaming services producing latest demonstrates, it should come as no surprise that the 2010s have an abundance of excellent miniseries.
  • The shows that have made the cut consist of everything from moody historical dramas to pulsating explorations of war, and even to cutting crime thrillers that keep audiences on the edge of their seats from start to finish.
  • A spiritual sequel to their 2001 masterpiece Band of Brothers, The Pacific sees Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks again taking small-screen drama to the front lines of WWII with an immersion into the Pacific Theater of the war that is as grueling as it is gripping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, serving as both the definitive peak of television’s golden era and the decade that saw the rampant rise in popularity of streaming services producing latest demonstrates, it should come as no surprise that the 2010s have an abundance of excellent miniseries. In fact, such is the quality of the miniseries of the decade; each year from 2010 to 2019 has an array of enthralling and memorable titles, with masterpieces like When They See Us, The Haunting of Hill House, and Unbelievable missing out on selection.

The shows that have made the cut consist of everything from moody historical dramas to pulsating explorations of war, and even to cutting crime thrillers that keep audiences on the edge of their seats from start to finish. Defined by their sharp writing, brilliant production value, and the enduring impact their stories have had on viewers, these miniseries represent television at its best throughout the 2010s.

A spiritual sequel to their 2001 masterpiece Band of Brothers, The Pacific sees Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks again taking small-screen drama to the front lines of WWII with an immersion into the Pacific Theater of the war that is as grueling as it is gripping. Following the experiences of three American soldiers from different regiments, the miniseries examines the chaos and carnage of the campaign, depicting battles such as Iwo Jima, Okinawa, and Guadalcanal.

In a recent development, earning universal acclaim for its visceral authenticity, The Pacific is a brutal masterpiece of war drama that soars on the back of its enormous production and the impact of its performances. Enriched by its endeavor to go beyond the ordeal of battle and explore the impact the war had on soldiers returning home, The Pacific is a contemplative and considered examination of those involved in the war. This breathtaking miniseries stands as yet another classic foray into the genre from Hanks and Spielberg.

At face value, 2011 was one of the weaker years of the decade for miniseries magnificence. However, it still contains some underappreciated gems, with Mildred Pierce serving as an overlooked drama defined by its adherence to its source material and a litany of powerful performances. The HBO-produced miniseries stars Kate Winslet as Mildred Pierce, a self-sacrificing single mother during the Great Depression who faces hardship as she tries to open a restaurant while striving to win the love and respect of her narcissistic eldest daughter.

Soaring off the back of Winslet’s Emmy Award-winning performance, Mildred Pierce finds an understated impact as a heartbreaking drama of love and desperation that is beautifully acted and delicately written. While some may argue its five-episode run is extensive and results in a number of lulls throughout the miniseries, Mildred Pierce emerges triumphant as one of 2011’s best small-screen offerings. This period piece immerses audiences in the rigors of Depression-era America and the many obstacles a single mother faced in such a time.

A three-part romantic drama exploring the impact the AIDS epidemic of the 1980s had on Stockholm’s gay community, Don’t Ever Wipe Tears Without Gloves excels with its artful presentation and delicate handling of its characters and their turmoil. Over the miniseries' three episodes, titled “Love,” “Diseases,” and “Death,” the miniseries follows 19-year-old Rasmus (Adam Pålsson) as he seeks out Stockholm’s gay community and begins a relationship with Benjamin (Adam Lundgren) after moving to the city from his rural home to attend university.

The series’ progression, including flashbacks to Rasmus’ childhood and flashforwards to his agonizing final days, is handled respectfully. The story is realized with a quiet visual beauty and powerful use of symbolism that both support the central story of Rasmus and Ben coming to terms with a damning AIDS diagnosis and illustrate the widespread fear and ignorance surrounding the disease at the time. Also incorporating how religious institutions responded to the disease and those suffering from it, Don’t Ever Wipe Tears Without Gloves is a powerful and profoundly human examination of a dark chapter in history marred by speculative terror and homophobia.

Another three-part miniseries from Europe, Generation War is a German WWII drama following the isolated experiences of five friends throughout the conflict. A tale of disillusionment, desperation, and violence, its focus on two soldiers, a nurse, an aspiring singer, and a Jewish man trying to flee the country is bolstered by its analysis of the corruption of totalitarianism. It doesn’t shirk the fact that a lot of Germans were in favor of Adolf Hitler’s vision of the world, only to be confronted with the hardship of surviving it.

In a recent development, while it has flaws, Generation War is defined by its striking maturity and ability to find sympathy in its main characters through their youthful naivety and brutal disenchantment. Its inherent appeals for forgiveness for those who felt helplessly complicit in the Nazi agenda may be misguided at times. However, the series showcases in unflinching fashion the harsh reality of war and the punishing final truth that, even for those who emerged from the conflict alive, there was little joy and no glory awaiting them at the end of the war.

Starring Frances McDormand and featuring an all-star supporting cast that includes Richard Jenkins, Jesse Plemons, Rachel Brosnahan, and Bill Murray, among others, Olive Kitteridge is a sorrowful, sweeping drama firmly focused on human connection. Based on Elizabeth Strout’s 2008 novel of the same name, the four-episode miniseries follows the titular Kitteridge, a retired schoolteacher with a misanthropic edge and underlying depression, and her strained familial relationships as they unfold over 25 years.

Industry observers note that the narrative runs at a slow and measured pace. In this meticulous tempo, the performances of the actors and the impact of the writing flourish, delivering a grounded drama that makes an impression through its sincerity and tenderness. At once bleak and uplifting, Olive Kitteridge is always compelling, delving into the minutiae of life’s complexity with an enticing character who, while sympathetic, is often the source of her problems.

In a recent development, adapted from Agatha Christie’s novel of the same name, And Then There Were None is something of an underrated gem of 2010s mystery television. Constantly intriguing with its notions of justice and punishment, it follows eight individuals as they converge on the isolated Soldier Island by invitation of a “Mr. and Mrs. Owen,” where they are seen by the island house’s caretakers. When one of the guests is killed, the others learn that they are ensnared in an elaborate ruse: each of them is responsible for an unjust death, and the killer—who is among them—has no intention of stopping until all of them are dead.

Recent findings suggest that as dashing as it is dark, the miniseries thrives on the talent of its ensemble cast and the misanthropic lens with which it views its characters. Loyal in plot and spirit to Christie’s 1939 novel, And Then There Were None offers intoxicating suspense and intrigue as it marries its psychological murder-mystery antics with an impressive rogues' gallery of amoral and corrupt characters.

An eight-part miniseries defined by its constant and weighted sense of tension and the impact of its performances, The Night Of is one of HBO’s defining triumphs in the wheelhouse of limited series entertainment. It follows Nasir (Riz Ahmed), an American-Pakistani college student accused of murdering a girl he hooked up with at a party. Amid the apparent hopelessness of his case, Nasir forms a bond with an inmate at Rikers Island, while public defender John Stone (John Turturro) represents "Naz", believing there is more to the murder case.

Sources indicate that thriving not only as a gripping murder mystery, but as a dramatic observation of the legal system rife with political overtones and a commentary on racism in America as well, The Night Of excels through its timely notes of social criticism as much as it does through its captivating suspense. It's further enriched by a detailed mystery that methodically unfolds and Nasir’s surprising coming-of-age story that unfurls behind bars. The miniseries is loaded with intrigue and interest that make it one of the more noteworthy efforts of the decade.

One of the best Western stories to have graced the screen in recent years, Godless excels as a typically violent and vivacious take on the genre that challenges its male-dominated history with a brilliantly conceived story that allows for a mostly female cast. The town of La Belle, populated almost exclusively by women after a mining accident killed most of the men, becomes the center of an outlaw’s vengeance when his prodigy, Roy Goode (Jack O’Connell), seeks refuge, having split off from his gang with a stash of money.

Industry observers note that the story takes a keen interest not only in Goode’s relationship with widowed rancher Alice Fletcher (Michelle Dockery), but also in several other figures within the town and the unique struggles they endure. Netflix's Godless is defined by its scope and ambition as well as its smart subversion of Western conventions. A confident piece of genre deconstruction that is often pulsating and quite tender when it needs to be, the Netflix original series tackles femininity in the Old West with compelling grit and refreshing insight to be a true highlight of 2010s television.

In a recent development, one of the most shocking series of any genre of the 2010s, Sharp Objects finds a compelling depth and striking unpredictability in its basis on Gillian Flynn’s debut novel of the same name. Amy Adams stars as Camille Preaker, a crime reporter who, after being released from a psychiatric hospital after battling alcoholism and depression, returns to her hometown to investigate the murders of two young girls. The disturbing nature of the case clashes with Camille’s strained relationships with her family, forcing her to confront her demons.

Bolstered by an array of exceptional performances, Sharp Objects is a true slow-burn tale that extracts every ounce of tension and drama from its story, entrancing viewers in the immersive allure of its bleak atmosphere rife with moments of agonizing suspense. Bereft of cat-and-mouse chaos or the tantalizing menace of a criminal mastermind, the series instead demands a typically brilliant turn from Adams to explore the full breadth of Camille’s internal struggles with deft drama and nuance. Unsurprisingly, the actress delivers in spades, compelling viewers for the entirety of the series’ eight-episode run and right up to its shocking climax.

Recent findings suggest that A true masterpiece of small-screen drama, Chernobyl is comfortably among the greatest miniseries of all time and saw the 2010s end in spectacular fashion from the perspective of television entertainment. The precise, procedural historical drama transpires in the aftermath of the Chernobyl nuclear plant disaster of 1986, focusing on the immediate clean-up efforts, the fear that the radiation emitted could impact most of mainland Europe, and the eventual trial to determine culpability for the avoidable catastrophe.

Realized with near-unbearable tension, the series thrives with its imposing scope. It runs as an all-encompassing dramatization of the many sacrificial acts that ensured the disaster didn’t exacerbate, and the political conniving that tried to conceal the truth for as long as possible. It is a masterpiece of creeping dread, an eye-opening display of real-world institutional corrosion, and one of the most absorbingly horrific stories that has ever been put to screen. It will endure as an vital masterwork for many years to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, HBO has been in the business of making instant classics for a long time now, and one of their latest additions is on track to do just that. There's no doubt that it's a tumultuous time for TV at large, and with the massive changes in terms of organization from parent companies running the show around HBO, some things are bound to fall through the cracks.

Well, despite significant changes like the Paramount Skydance takeover of brands like Warner Bros., and the fact that the DCU's future is hanging in the balance with the removal of James Gunn and Peter Safran as the co-heads of DC Studios, the Lanterns series is poised to have a long and healthy reputation as one of the best entries in the DCU.

With the incredible Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre investing a great deal of time and effort into crafting and refining their iterations of Hal Jordan and John Stewart respectively, it's good to see that Lanterns is likely to age like fine wine, especially when many of the other DCU projects, such as Creature Commandos, Supergirl, and Peacemaker season 2 all left audiences with questions about what the future holds.

Sources indicate that one of the greatest strengths of the Lanterns series, and one that is sure to help it continue to resonate with audiences into the future, is the fact that it's a self-contained story that is complete after eight episodes. Sure, there are some threads that could still be picked up, but the heart of the story is resolved, and audiences leave satisfied with the resolution presented by the finale.

Where many of the other DCU stories were designed to help build the wider universe and establish characters and connections that would ultimately play an important role in the overarching story, Lanterns was concerned with telling Hal and John's story.

Sources indicate that and by the end of the series, the way this relationship developed, the mysteries established early in the series, and the antagonists who created unrest and distress, were all put to rest. Ultimately, it's a buddy cop drama with a core mystery and some superhero elements that lift the story from the typical to the extraordinary.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, with Gunn's exit as the architect of the DCU, there is a high degree of uncertainty about what is next for the world he helped to shape from its latest beginning with Creature Commandos. Jeremy Latcham now stands to guide the DC Universe forward, but whether he chooses to discard many of the characters and stories that have been set up remains to be seen.

Despite all of that, Lanterns doesn't really need to do anything else to prove itself. Creature Commandos was clearly setting up a bigger story in the DCU. Superman and Supergirl both worked to establish the most powerful heroes on planet Earth, and Peacemaker season 2 bridged the gaps between the DCEU and the DCU while also setting up a larger plot for Chapter 1: Gods and Monsters.

Lanterns was less focused on building the rest of the DCU, and more concerned with creating a strong standalone story around Hal and John, which it accomplished. The focus on a character study rather than placing a piece into the DCU puzzle paid off, and regardless of what's next, it works.

In a recent development, but, there is a strong possibility that the Lanterns story will continue despite James Gunn's exit. As mentioned above, Jeremy Latcham has been assigned to reinvigorate the DCU, and to infuse some of the MCU magic he learned as an executive at Marvel Studios into this world of stories.

It's likely that Latcham will try to hold onto whatever worked in the DCU, and enhance the best parts of this universe while quietly shelving the things that no longer fit. While there is a strong possibility that the narratives that rely most on Gunn's control, such as Creature Commandos and whatever story is born out of the Peacemaker season 2 finale, Lanterns is in a very different position.

Sources indicate that the creative team that put Lanterns together was not directly controlled by Gunn. And beyond that, Lanterns has proven to be one of the most well-received entries in the DCU to date. As a result, it's very likely that Lanterns and characters like John Stewart as played by Aaron Pierre will survive into whatever the next chapter of the DCU looks like.

  • Industry observers note that "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010.
  • According to recent reports, if you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, unless you've been living under a rock for multiple decades, you've probably heard of "The Hunger Games." Written by Suzanne Collins, this hybrid of "Battle Royale" and reality television hit shelves in 2008 and introduced readers around the world to Katniss Everdeen, a young woman trying to support her family with illegal game hunting in the deeply impoverished District 12 of a reformed North America known as Panem. When Katniss' beloved younger sister Primrose is chosen, or "reaped," via a random lottery to participate in the annual Games (where two "tributes" from all 12 districts are forced to compete to the death on live television until one victor emerges), Katniss volunteers as tribute, and her time as a Hunger Games participant begins.

Industry observers note that "The Hunger Games" kicked off the property of the same name and was followed by sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay," released in 2009 and 2010. Naturally, a "Hunger Games" film franchise followed in 2012 and spawned four blockbusters. ("Mockingjay" got split into two parts, something that director Francis Lawrence regrets.) Then, in 2020, Collins released her first literary "Hunger Games" prequel, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — which centers on the origin story of future Panem president Coriolanus Snow — and five years later, we got "Sunrise on the Reaping," which explains precisely how Katniss' eventual friend and mentor (and her fellow District 12 victor) Haymitch Abernathy won his Games.

According to recent reports, if you've already read all of the "Hunger Games" books and seen all the movies (including the pretty great movie version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," which is now out in theaters), what should you check out next? From dystopian classics to other YA favorites, we've got some ideas.

According to recent reports, A lot of dystopian novels are referred to as "speculative fiction," which means that the scenario laid out by the author could conceivably happen in real life ... so, let's hope that Nana Kwame Adjei-Brenyah's novel "Chain-Gang All-Stars" doesn't come to pass. Released in 2023, this novel imagines a world where the incarceration system in the United States is, somehow, even worse than it is in our reality — in that prisoners are allowed to enroll in a program called CAPE, which stands for "Criminal Action Penal Entertainment." Not only are the inmates in CAPE constantly monitored (with their every move broadcast to hungry audiences), they're also sent across the country to constantly participate in gladiator matches against each other that are, you guessed it, televised as well. The book's title comes from the reimagined version of a traditional "chain gang," where the prisoner-gladiators are called "Links" and given two options to leave: either they're High Freed, meaning released, or Low Freed, meaning killed.

It has been revealed that throughout "Chain-Gang All-Stars," we follow the Angola-Hammond Chain in the system and, more specifically, Hamara "Hurricane Staxxx" Stacker and Loretta "Blood Mama" Thurwar, the two female fighters in a secret relationship who open the book. As we move through the unsettling world Adjei-Brenyah concocted in "Chain-Gang All Stars," we follow a wide variety of prisoners participating in this gut-wrenching game ... and it's sort of impossible to not think of the "Hunger Games" franchise as you read it, albeit in a good way. After you wrap up all five "Hunger Games" books, check out "Chain-Gang All-Stars." (Nina Starner).

When it comes to seeing people die horrible deaths in death games televised for the entertainment of an oppressive ruling class, no book does it on a larger scale than Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl." The book takes place after Earth has been taken over by an alien corporation that seeks to mine the planet for resources. Those who aren't killed during the initial invasion are then forced to compete in an intergalactic reality show program, an RPG-like "dungeon crawl" where they have to navigate various levels of a labyrinthian dungeon, each filled with increasingly dangerous monsters and scenarios.

What makes "Dungeon Crawler Carl" unique is how it blends together ridiculous video game and tabletop RPG logic with an unhealthy dose of pop culture references, the humor of a Douglas Adams book, and the brutality and social commentary about unchecked capitalism and authoritarianism of "The Hunger Games." Indeed, reading Dinniman's book and its follow-ups is like playing a fun RPG session, in that it's chaotic, messy, hilarious, and weird, all while packing a serious emotional punch full of heartbreak and cruel twists and turns. But rather than reveling in their misery, Dinniman's characters rage against the corporate machine in an effort to break it. What you end up with is a story about the necessity of resistance and the importance of community, both of which are themes that will resonate with "Hunger Games" fans. And did I mention it features an endlessly quotable talking cat? (Rafael Motamayor).

It has been revealed that I don't think it's possible to have a conversation about young adult dystopian books and films like the "Hunger Games" stories without discussing "The Handmaid's Tale." Margaret Atwood's landmark 1980 book set a standard for dystopian narratives rivaled only by George Orwell's "1984," but Atwood's specificity is what makes her imagined world so terrifying — in that "The Handmaid's Tale" takes place in a world where a religious totalitarian regime oppresses women and queer people. Offred (meaning "of Fred"), our heroine, works as one of the titular handmaids, which means she's prized for her fertility and used as a "vessel" (that's putting it politely) for her Commander, Fred, to impregnate instead of his un-fertile wife. As Offred exists in Gilead (which forbids women from having quite literally any rights and punishes them with death if they even try to stray), we follow her every move in the novel, learning bits and pieces about her life before Gilead as June, a mother and wife with the freedom to live as she pleased.

"The Handmaid's Tale" was adapted into a Hulu series in 2017, and while I do think Elisabeth Moss did an incredible job playing Offred, the show ran through Atwood's book by the end of Season 1 and kept its wheels spinning for, in my opinion, far too long (although it at least gets its final message right.) If you haven't read Atwood's book but are familiar with its well-known red costumes and overall vibe, I couldn't possibly recommend it more. Its prose is beautiful, its subject matter is terrifying, and it's a clear precursor to and inspiration for the stories found in the "Hunger Games" franchise. (Nina Starner).

Though certainly not as dark in tone as "The Hunger Games," the pop culture celebration that is author Ernest Cline's "Ready Player One" is an oddly fitting companion piece for fans of the world Suzanne Collins built. One could even look at it as a bit of a palette cleanser, albeit one that still scratches a similar itch.

Industry observers note that for those not familiar, the book takes place in 2044 and focuses on Wade Watts, who spends his days in the virtual utopia known as the OASIS. Wade's devoted his life to studying the puzzles hidden within this world's digital confines, themselves based on their creator's fixation on pop culture — with the promise of massive power and fortune to whoever can unlock them.

Industry observers note that "Ready Player One" is jam-packed with pop culture references and is lighthearted in a lot of ways. However, it's also terribly dystopian, as the OASIS is not only people's sole escape from the harsh realities of the outside world, there's very little person-to-person communication anymore outside of the virtual space. Beyond that, the rush to solve the puzzles and nab the fortune results in a deadly game for Wade and many others, which is where the "Hunger Games" of it all comes in.

In a recent development, steven Spielberg's 2018 movie adaptation left a lot to be desired for many fans and, yes, a "Ready Player Two" movie was in the works in 2021, though it's yet to materialize. Setting the film aside, the novel remains a true gem filled with wonderful world building, fully-realized characters, and just a dash of "kill or be killed" to make the whole thing extra exciting, elevating it beyond the barrage of references it might have otherwise been. (Ryan Scott).

In a recent development, the funny thing about Pierce Brown's "Red Rising" series is that the first book in the still-ongoing saga is very much a "Hunger Games" riff ... until it's not. Set in a distant future where humanity has been rigidly split into various genetically modified castes that determine a person's role in society, the story follows Darrow, a young Martian "red" whose wife is murdered by the ruling "gold" regime, sending him on a quest for revenge that ultimately spans the entire solar system. But before the sweeping space opera can begin, Darrow infiltrates the gold caste and must survive the Institute, a deadly school where young people are violently set against one another in not-so-simulated combat and conquest.

Industry observers note that those who enjoyed the blend of youthful angst, action, sci-fi world-building, and dystopian politics of "The Hunger Games" will take quickly and easily to "Red Rising," which offers a similar flavor with a harsher, more masculine edge. However, starting with the second book "Golden Son" and continuing into later installments, Brown takes things in a wholly upcoming direction, turning his Suzanne Collins riff into the kind of sprawling, detailed, intense, and morally murky epic that would make Frank Herbert and George R.R. Martin proud. This is the perfect stepping stone for "Hunger Games" fans hoping to branch out into a different flavor of science fiction. It's familiar enough, until it is suddenly, and brutally, not. (Jacob Hall).

GTA: Boston Would Go Wicked Hard, Kid

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that considering that Grand Theft Auto 6 just debuted after a 13-year wait, it’s safe to say that we won’t be getting another one any time soon.
  • Industry observers note that that’s right suckers, Miami and Los Angeles’ time is over.
  • Industry observers note that the thing that really makes GTA 6 so special is Leonida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that considering that Grand Theft Auto 6 just debuted after a 13-year wait, it’s safe to say that we won’t be getting another one any time soon. That’s fine, because Leonida is so enormous that I know I’ll still be finding secrets in it years from now. And yet, I can’t help myself. I’m already wondering where the series could possibly go next. Allow me to offer one unsolicited idea: Massachusetts.

Industry observers note that that’s right suckers, Miami and Los Angeles’ time is over. It’s time to let me drive a sports car down the Freedom Trail as I barrel through Boston blasting Dropkick Murphys. You can chalk this up to a little Thanksgiving homesickness, as I wasn’t able to travel to my home state for the holiday, but I am convinced I am on to something here.

Industry observers note that the thing that really makes GTA 6 so special is Leonida. Rockstar’s digital recreation of Florida is a perfect playground for GTA’s sandbox chaos, and it takes advantage of the state’s geographical diversity to do that. You’ve got a bustling Miami to build on for Vice City, but you also have a mix of run-down towns, rural farmlands, beaches, and quiet islands. That wide array of locations makes for a more varied GTA experience, as you bounce between areas with very different speeds.

You know what other state has that feel? Massachusetts, baby! You’ve got Boston at the heart of it all, a historic city that’s unlike any Rockstar has ever recreated. Just outside the city limits, you’ve got a host of quaint suburban towns filled with shopping malls and banks. Go west, and you’ll end up in the deep wilderness, just as you find yourself in when you go north in Leonida. On the east side, you’ve got Cape Cod, a vacation getaway built on a fishing economy. And just off the coast, you’ve got scenic islands like Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket. Boil all of that down into a tight GTA map, and you’ve got all the same basic ingredients that make Leonida fun to explore, but in a state that looks and feels very different.

Rockstar is no stranger to the region, either. 2006’s Bully was set in a fictional town in New England. Even though that was 20 years ago, Rockstar nailed the feeling of suburban ennui that exists throughout the state. It’s easy to see how the team could recapture that spirit by including its own take on Harvard in a GTA game. Hell, why not just make the town of Bullworth canon to GTA?

There’s more to Leonida than its landmarks, of course. Florida also makes for a great GTA setting because it’s full of the kind of strange Americans Rockstar loves to lampoon. GTA 6 gets to play around with conspiracy theorists, right-wing gun nuts, rich playboys, and more in its wide cultural satire.

It has been revealed that well guess what? Massachusetts is full of ripe comedic targets too! Within Boston alone, you’ve got your pick of loudmouthed bros who always seem eager to get into a bar fight. That’s contrasted with wealthy retirees living in beach bubbles, hustling Italian-Americans in Boston’s North End, artsy communities in towns like Northampton, and so much more. There’s so much to satirize beyond your typical Masshole, even though Rockstar could have a field day poking fun at the accent.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Sources indicate that more than anything, I’m dying to see Boston’s obsessive sports culture make its way into GTA. You get some nods to the real sports world of Miami in GTA 6, but it would most assuredly be the central focus of a Boston-set game full of loudmouthed Red Sox and Patriots fans. Let me go to Gillette Stadium and plow through Patriot Place in a bulldozer, cowards! And considering how much Rockstar enjoys lampooning current cultural trends, there’s even fertile ground to dig into the rise of sports betting and treat it as a criminal enterprise. I mean, Rockstar must be licking its lips at the prospect of making a fake Kalshi, right?

My wishlist of things I’d love to see in Grand Theft Massachusetts is long: Faneuil Hall! Boston Dynamics! Logan Airport! I’m sure that people from just about any other state in America feel the same way about their home. So much of the fun of GTA 6 is getting such a wide view of Florida that really emphasizes how diverse a single state can be. It’s easy to flatten them out, judging them by their cultural urban epicenters or voting demographics, but a good road trip will show you just how vibrant even the smallest pockets of the country can be. Every state deserves to be roasted as bad as Florida.

Apple's latest flagship smartwatch, the Apple Watch Series 12, is worth the upgrade. With this model, Apple has upgraded the processor, added a latest heart rate sensor, and improved the display durability. It's certainly one of Apple's best smartwatches, but that also means it isn't cheap: All these new features give the new Series 12 a starting price of $399, which only increases if you choose a model with cellular data. However, for Black Friday, you can take up to $100 off the Series 12, bringing the starting price down to $299.

The three biggest hardware upgrades with the Apple Watch Series 12 are the heart rate sensor, the S11 chip, and Ceramic Shield 2. That heart rate sensor now checks your pulse every five seconds, or 20 times a minute. Apple states the Series 12 checks your heart rate variability 24 times more than the Series 11, and your background heart rate 60 times more frequently than the Series 11. The company is even so bold as to say the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate monitor on a wearable.

Powering the newly introduced heart rate monitor is the S11 chip, Apple's latest processor for the Apple Watch. The S11 isn't only responsible for these new heart rate features, however. In addition to running the same watchOS 27 features as other compatible Apple Watches, the S11 on the Series 12 can run Audio Intelligence, Apple's new suite of AI-powered audio features. That includes "Live Rewind," which lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation, and "Siri Recaps," which displays summaries of your conversations throughout the day. Finally, the other major advantage with the Series 12 is Ceramic Shield 2. This is a display upgrade that Apple typically reserves for more premium Apple Watch finishes, but this year, the aluminum Series 12 gets it as well. That means the watch should be more durable against scratches and cracks, without you having to upgrade to the more expensive model.

In a recent development, how much you'll save on a Series 12 depends on the size, color, and model. At this time, Amazon is selling certain colors of the 42mm Series 12 for $299, while certain colors of the 46mm option run $449 (also marked down by $100). You can also save on the cellular models as well: The 42mm option is currently $429 (down from $499), while the 46mm model is $449 (down from $549).

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "The Hunger Games" franchise is back with a story fans have been waiting a very long time for.
  • It has been revealed that "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place on the "Hunger Games" timeline 24 years before the events of the first movie.
  • Plenty of "Hunger Games" characters return in this prequel in younger form, including Caesar Flickerman (played by Oscar winner Kieran Culkin) and Effie Trinket (played by Emmy nominee Elle Fanning).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"The Hunger Games" franchise is back with a story fans have been waiting a very long time for. "Sunrise on the Reaping" is the darkest movie in "The Hunger Games" series, flashing back to the famed games in which Haymitch Abernathy won. Originally played by Woody Harrelson, that character is a fan-favorite, but this movie does a lot of work to help fill in crucial elements of his character, played this time by Joseph Zada.

It has been revealed that "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place on the "Hunger Games" timeline 24 years before the events of the first movie. It follows sixteen-year-old Haymitch from District 12, beginning on the morning of the reaping for the 50th Annual Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell, the biggest Games yet with twice as many tributes. But Haymitch isn't the only classic character who gets more time to shine in this entry.

Plenty of "Hunger Games" characters return in this prequel in younger form, including Caesar Flickerman (played by Oscar winner Kieran Culkin) and Effie Trinket (played by Emmy nominee Elle Fanning). But they're not the only ones who will be familiar to fans of the series. There's also the matter of Mags Flanagan, a very vital character in the history of both the books and the movies. Originally played by Lynn Cohen in "Catching Fire," she won the 11th Hunger Games and volunteered as tribute during the 75th games.

This time around, the younger version of Cohen is played by actress Lili Taylor. The role is crucial, as Mags is the one who mentors Haymitch en route to his time in the games. But for those who feel Taylor looks familiar, there's a good reason for that: She's a great actress with one heck of a resume.

Lili Taylor got her start as an actress in the late '80s/early '90s, starring in movies such as "Mystic Pizza," "Say Anything," and "Born on the Fourth of July." She worked steadily throughout the '90s in movies, in addition to doing some television, including an episode of "The X-Files." Some of her other notable credits from this period include "Ransom" and "The Haunting.".

In a recent development, one of her earliest, substantial breakout roles came in the early 2000s on "Six Feet Under," one of the best HBO shows of all time, as Lisa Kimmel. She also continued to work very steadily in movies during this period, earning credits in "Brooklyn's Finest" and "Public Enemies," among others. Though not often in the spotlight as a lead, Taylor tends to use her talents in memorable supporting roles.

According to recent reports, the 2010s were particularly kind to Taylor. 2013's "The Conjuring" kicked off the biggest non-Marvel cinematic universe, and she had a major part to play as Carolyn Perron, one of the heads of the household at the center of that movie's haunting. It's arguably her most notable role to date. She reprised the role in "The Nun" and "The Conjuring: Last Rites." That same year, she also starred in "Hemlock Grove," one of the first original reveals produced by Netflix.

Taylor has over 100 credits to her name so we can't possibly go over all of them, but some other titles viewers might recognize her from include "The Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials," "Leatherface," HBO's "Perry Mason," "Outer Range," "Fear Street: Prom Queen," and most recently Marvel's "Daredevil: Born Again," where she played Marge McCaffrey.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are plenty of reasons Peacock’s The Good Daughter is so damn watchable.
  • Recent findings suggest that you want buried secrets?
  • According to recent reports, like The Good Daughter, Dark Places is anchored by a sibling relationship reshaped by the impact of horrifying violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are plenty of reasons Peacock’s The Good Daughter is so damn watchable. The performances, for one—Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are terrific as estranged sisters Sam and Charlotte Quinn. But it’s also a great story, tracing the corrosive effect of a years-ago trauma on the women and their lawyer father (Brendan Gleeson) amid the slow revelation of many extremely dark secrets. If you want more of that flavor of trauma-driven drama with a tight focus on family bonds, there’s one movie you should watch: 2015's Dark Places.

Recent findings suggest that you want buried secrets? Dark Places has seriously buried secrets. Adapted from the Gillian Flynn novel, the film follows Libby Day (Charlize Theron), who survived the mass murder of her family in 1985. The crime is blamed on her brother Ben, a moody loner whose conviction was based in large part on Libby’s own testimony. For a long time, Libby is financially sustained by donations from people who sympathize with her plight, but three decades after the murders, the money has dried up, and Libby is desperate—so desperate, she agrees to help out a “true crime” club that believes her brother is innocent and is working toward his release.

According to recent reports, like The Good Daughter, Dark Places is anchored by a sibling relationship reshaped by the impact of horrifying violence. Libby and Ben’s experience mirrors Sam and Charlie’s in many ways, including in the way both Libby and Ben carry secrets for years after the terrible events that took family from them. The stories are also both compelling mysteries, slowly revealing the shocking truths behind one horrific night, and ultimately allowing the characters to better understand one another.

Sources indicate that dark Places also explores the insular, suffocating nature of small-town life, and how rumor and gossip become a poisonous presence in people’s lives. Libby, Ben, Sam, and Charlie all have to deal with others' assumptions and revelations that they've been betrayed by those closest to them, leading to powerful resolutions. If you loved The Good Daughter, you’ll love this movie. Stream Dark Places on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that want more stories about family dynamics around secrets, violence, and explosive emotional confrontations? Here are a few more movies fans of The Good Daughter are bound to enjoy.

There’s no violent crime at the heart of this slow-burn drama—just an explosive chaos agent named Kym, played by Anne Hathaway. If your favorite aspect of The Good Daughter was the relationship between sisters Sam and Charlie, then this movie is perfect. Released from rehab to attend her sister’s wedding, Kym is self-hating, angry, and haunted by a terrible event from her childhood. Her sister, Rachel (Rosemary DeWitt), is welcoming, but has never truly forgiven Kym, and the simmering tension between the sisters and the rest of the family drives a drama that you won’t be able to look away from. Stream Rachel Getting Married on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that if you really vibed on the Southern setting, the slow-burn mystery, and the exploration of flawed justice in the modern age depicted in The Good Daughter, check out Where the Crawdads Sing. It’s a slower, dreamier rumination on rural life, violence and its cost, and small-town justice, but it hits the same sweet spot in its story about a woman named Kya (Daisy Edgar-Jones) who was raised in an isolated house in the swamps of North Carolina. Accused in 1969 of a murder, Kya’s story stretches back to her childhood, when she’s slowly abandoned by her entire family, leaving her at age seven to survive on her own. Ostracized as the “swamp girl” by the town, Kya fights to live her life and be loved while facing the unwanted—and violently persistent—attention of the murder victim. It’s about broken families, deeply buried secrets, and what we do to survive. Stream Where the Crawdads Sing on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that the Good Daughter is about life in a small, Southern town, family trauma, and the legal system—which makes A Time to Kill the perfect movie to watch when you finish the show. When a Black man’s daughter is sexually assaulted in Mississippi and her attackers—local members of the Ku Klux Klan—look likely to go free, he violently and publicly murders them. Local lawyer Jake Brigance (Matthew McConaughey) takes on the case, assisted by law student Ellen Roark (Sandra Bullock). They face violent opposition, withering racism, and an unfair legal system that echoes the environment in The Good Daughter in ways fans will appreciate. Stream A Time to Kill on YoutTube or rent it on Prime Video.

The Dry might be as close as you can get to The Good Daughter in terms of tone and story. Although set in Australia instead of the American South, The Dry is a story driven by past crimes and buried secrets in a rural setting just like the show. Twenty years ago, Federal agent Aaron Falk (Eric Bana) fled his hometown when he was suspected of the murder of his girlfriend. When his childhood friend, Luke, appears to have murdered his wife and young son before killing himself, he returns to investigate. The slow revelation of two mysteries—one in the past and one simmering in the drought-stricken present—makes this an ideal companion film to the show. Stream The Dry on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

Set in Boston instead of the South, and focused on male friendships instead of a sisters’ bond, Mystic River nevertheless nails the same atmosphere of dread as The Good Daughter. In 1975, boyhood friends Jimmy, Dave, and Sean are traumatized when Dave is abducted and assaulted by two men. In 1990, the three men remain connected in their Boston neighborhood—Jimmy (Sean Penn) is an ex-convict still connected to local crime, Sean (Kevin Bacon) is a State Police detective, and Dave (Tim Robbins) is a blue-collar worker still haunted by his experience. When Jimmy’s daughter is found murdered and Dave seems implicated, Sean and Jimmy launch investigations from either side of the law, with Dave’s fate hanging in the balance. The ending is powerfully brutal, but this story of secrets and suspicion will resonate with fans of the show. Rent Mystic River on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the holiday season upon us and the 2026 movie calendar winding down, there are a handful of the best Christmas movies I return to every December, and Elf is pretty much guaranteed to make the list. Will Ferrell running around Newly introduced York City in yellow tights, eating spaghetti covered in candy and screaming about Santa Claus has become as much a part of the holidays as putting up the tree. According to one of the movie's stars, Hollywood wasn't exactly convinced it had a future Christmas classic on its hands back in 2003.

According to recent reports, andy Richter, who played Morris in the Jon Favreau-directed comedy, recently reflected on the making of Elf and explained why the movie was considered something of a gamble. Speaking with People while promoting his new book, Elf: Unwrapped, which he co-wrote with Aaron Karo, Richter stated the movie's eventual success makes it easy to forget just how uncertain things were when production began.

It was a risky movie, and nobody thinks about that because it’s now a classic, but at the time there was nobody that was aching to make a movie with Will Ferrell as the star or with Jon Favreau as the director, for that matter.

Recent findings suggest that considering Will Ferrell himself had doubts when he first tried on Buddy's iconic costume, I can understand why some studio executives might have been nervous. At the time, the SNL alum was best known for his work on Saturday Night Live, where he'd spent seven seasons establishing himself as one of the show's biggest stars. He'd appeared in movies like Old School and Zoolander, but he hadn't yet proven he could carry a major studio comedy as its leading man.

Industry observers note that favreau, meanwhile, had directed the 2001 comedy Made, but he was still relatively inexperienced behind the camera. According to Richter, the studio was taking a chance on both men. He added:.

They were rolling the dice with this movie and it really paid off.

It's funny to think about now, considering Ferrell went on to become one of the biggest comedy stars of the 2000s, while Favreau would eventually direct Iron Man, helping launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe. He's also had a major hand in shaping the modern Star Wars franchise with The Mandalorian. But back in 2003, the idea of giving a relatively untested leading man a Christmas comedy about a grown man raised by elves probably sounded pretty ridiculous on paper. And considering some of the behind-the-scenes stories about making Elf, it's remarkable how well everything came together. It is a ridiculous premise. That's a big part of why I love it.

Sources indicate that richter also credited the combination of Ferrell's comedic instincts and Favreau's approach to storytelling for making the movie work. Interestingly, though, the movie’s star recently addressed the longstanding rumors about his relationship with Favreau during the production. It seems there's still plenty to learn about what went into making this particular Christmas classic. As for Richter, he told the outlet that the film succeeds because:.

The combination of their two sensibilities, which we go into in the book, that really made it work because it’s funny, but also has a lot of heart.

I think that's a pretty accurate assessment. Ferrell gets to be completely absurd as Buddy, whether he's congratulating a coffee shop for having the world's best cup of coffee or trying to navigate a revolving door. Yet the movie also gives us a genuinely sweet story about a guy looking for his father and trying to find somewhere he belongs.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Recent findings suggest that james Caan's performance as Walter Hobbs deserves some credit here, too. His perpetually irritated reaction to Buddy's enthusiasm makes their relationship work, and without that dynamic, I don't think the movie would have nearly the same emotional payoff. Whatever reservations Hollywood had about the project, audiences certainly didn't share them once it arrived in theaters.

It has been revealed that according to The Numbers, Elf opened to more than $31 million during its first weekend in November 2003. It has since earned approximately $234 million worldwide, including revenue from subsequent theatrical releases. That's a pretty impressive return for a movie with a reported $32 million production budget.

The movie was successful enough that Hollywood naturally wanted another one, though Ferrell has since explained why he walked away from a potentially lucrative Elf sequel.

According to recent reports, more than two decades later, it's difficult to imagine the holiday season without Buddy the Elf. The movie remains a favorite among families, and people are still finding fresh things to appreciate about it, including one particularly interesting question about Buddy's journey from the North Pole to New York City.

Sources indicate that I find it interesting that a movie nobody could guarantee would succeed has become something people practically schedule their Christmas celebrations around. Ferrell has made plenty of successful comedies since, and Favreau's career has gone places nobody could have predicted in 2003.

There's something special about Elf. Considering how many Christmas movies come and go without making much of an impression, I suspect the people who took that gamble are pretty happy they did.

Elf is streaming with a Hulu subscription.

The release of Fallout 5 is still a very long time away, with almost all of Bethesda Entertainment's focus on getting The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel into the hands of the public as promptly as possible, which is understandable given that Skyrim released all the way back in 2011.

Sources indicate that until then, we're going to have to get our fill of the post-apocalypse in other ways, and one of the best approaches to that is to simply go back and play the older games. That remarked, you can't be blamed for having explored every little nook and cranny that those releases have to offer already, but that's where the franchise's extensive modding community comes into play. With that in mind, if you're a Fallout: Fresh Vegas PC player, there's one upcoming mod release that you should absolutely be aware of heading into next year.

The developers behind Fallout Chicago, a huge DLC-sized mod for Fallout: Upcoming Vegas, have put out a roadmap for their process, and they're aiming to have all three acts of the main story complete and out there for the public to play by the latter half of 2027.

That comes after the team released an extensive demo for the game, which basically allows players to work through the entirety of the game's first act, as well as a bunch of side quests, and new points of interest to explore. As you might expect, there's a certain mob element that's set to feature heavily, with the mod description reading as follows:.

According to recent reports, "Fallout Chicago is a DLC sized expansion to the critically acclaimed Fallout Latest Vegas. You'll set out to solve pre-war mysteries, post-war politics between The Union Mob and Midwest Brotherhood along with other factions dilemmas. Chicago is dangerous and fraught with betrayal. Do you have what it takes to make it out on your mission? Hell, this was supposed to be a side job after all?".

It's a very cool and lore-appropriate premise, and one that could end up being an all-time great example of modding, if things pan out the way they're supposed to over the next year or so.

If it wasn't obvious already,Fallout Chicagois a bit of a love letter to the franchise overall, taking it to a location thatplayers have actually been requestingfrom Bethesda for a long time. Hopefully the popularity of the mod gives them pause for thought in their approach to the next game, as a full release set in the Windy City could be a brilliant next step for the series.

It has been revealed that of course, we do know that there's lots of official Fallout to come from Bethesda over the next few years. The studio has shifted focus to its biggest IP. That means we'll also be getting remasters of Fallout: New Vegas and Fallout 3, a brand-new entry from Obsidian, and Fallout 5. Exactly when these projects will release, I couldn't possibly say. So, in the meantime, I'd look to Fallout Chicago as your next significant fix.

His attempts to become a slightly more legitimate businessman have been complicated by the fact that some of Tulsa's supposedly legitimate businessmen aren't much better than him, and we've still got another four episodes to see how that all plays out this year.

The seventh episode of Tulsa King Season 4, titled "Black Diamonds," will officially premiere on Paramount+ tomorrow, Friday, November 27, at 3 a.m. ET. There are ten episodes in the fourth season, with the finale, "Exit Interview," scheduled to arrive on December 18, so we'll have wrapped things up with Dwight for the year by Christmas.

It has been revealed that there's no need to worry about whether we'll be seeing Stallone again next year, either, given that Paramount+ renewed the series for a fifth season before the fourth had even premiered. Interestingly, production on Season 5 is moving to Newly introduced York, the city Dwight was effectively banished from when we first met him.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

In a recent development, you thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

Industry observers note that you carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Created by Taylor Sheridan, with Boardwalk Empire creator Terence Winter serving as head writer, the series features Stallone (Rocky) as Dwight Manfredi, Martin Starr (Silicon Valley) as Bodhi, Jay Will (The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel) as Tyson Mitchell, Garrett Hedlund (TRON: Legacy) as Mitch Keller, Dana Delany (Body of Proof) as Margaret Devereaux, Frank Grillo (The Purge: Anarchy) as Bill Bevilaqua, Neal McDonough (Justified) as Cal Thresher, and Gretchen Mol (Boardwalk Empire) as Amanda Clark.

The story from the show's fourth season pitted the crew of Voyager against a unique threat that tested their perseverance more than any previous enemy had.

Now, new DLC for survival game Star Trek: Voyager - Across the Unknown​​​​​​​ will revisit the iconic storyline. Players won't just be able to relive "Year of Hell," however, they'll be able to change the course of history.​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that daedalic Entertainment has unveiled that the fourth Expansion Pass DLC for Across the Unknown will be inspired by "Year of Hell". The announcement describes the DLC as "a self-contained mini-campaign of three upcoming sectors." The DLC will be released on Dec. 9. As in the show​​​​​​​, the game will pit players against the Krenim captain Annorax as he wields a weapon that allows him to alter history and destroy entire species. As a standalone expansion, Year of Hell won't affect any of players' main-game save files​​​​​​​.

Unlike the base game, which sees the Voyager trying to rebuild​​​​​​​ and survive with few resources, Year of Hell will invert the traditional gameplay experience. Players will start with a fully repaired and fully equipped ship​​​​​​​ before encountering the Krenim. While damaged rooms will be repairable, lost decks will cause players to lose every room, and players can lose up to five decks​​​​​​​. Crew members can also die, leaving the Voyager crew scrambling to stay alive​​​​​​​. Daedalic Entertainment says that the goal of the DLC "isn't to finish with a perfect ship. It's to see how many of your crew are still standing after twelve months.".

According to recent reports, if players want to follow the plot of the "Year of Hell" episodes, that is absolutely possible, but Daedalic​​​​​​​ has given players another option. While Captain Janeway can make alliances with a number of friendly ships, she can also choose to join Annorax. "Help Annorax repair the timeline, once he agrees to stop erasing civilizations. Whether he keeps that promise is another matter. Your senior officers may not share your enthusiasm, and their disapproval grows as the months pass.".

It has been revealed that depending on which path players take​​​​​​​, the other inhabitants of the sectors will have shifting opinions of the Voyager and act accordingly. The base game is required, but those who own the Expansion Pass will automatically receive Year of Hell when it is released. In the meantime, you can rewatch the "Year of Hell" episodes​​​​​​​ to prepare for your own fight against Annorax.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that "South Park" has been on a roll recently. When the show finally left behind its Mr.-Garrison-as-Trump allegory and stopped doing endless specials (even if most of those were fantastic), it found its stride again in Season 28, which took on AI and deepfakes in the funniest way possible. Then, Season 29 took on everything from the data centers, to "looksmaxxing" and "aura farming" in a hilarious "Backrooms" parody, to club sports in a great "Heated Rivalry" parody, to the US beef shortage, and more.

It's been a funny season, and it's been a heartfelt season at times, particularly when the show killed Kenny (again) and decided to replace him with none other than a kid version of Randy (complete with mustache). It has even been a romantic season, with the Tweek and Craig romance-focused episode. What "South Park" usually isn't, however, is scary. That changed with the Season 29 finale, which delivered the scariest TV scene of 2026 — twice.

In the finale, "City Endings," the town of South Park (renamed this season as South America) is hit with major power outages that disrupt the town's "GTA VI" gametime. It is part of a conspiracy involving secret deals the government made with billionaire weenies. At the same time, there's paranoia involving supposed Chinese spies and possible cyberattacks from that country.

It has been revealed that in the middle of all this, Cartman, Stan, and Kyle are also haunted by visions of the late Kenny, who died after being blown up by an e-bike in the season's premiere. Except this is not just Kenny, but a zombified version that haunts the boys in the form of horrific ghouls that even infiltrate "GTA VI," like a spectre out of "The Ring.".

"South Park" has toyed with the horror genre before, usually body horror. There was the Michael Jackson parody with Mr. Jefferson slowly rotting away, for example, or the HumanCentipad. The Season 29 finale, however, features one of the wildest and most gruesome eldritch abominations in the nearly 30-year history of the show. It starts with several scenes of Kenny simply standing creepily in the background, stalking the boys as if to try and send a message.

"City Endings" is a legit horror episode, which is rare from the show that spent nearly a decade on a silly weed farm storyline. The image of Kenny just standing in the background, his face obscured by his hoodie but with bright eyes just shining like Pennywise in "It," is already quite disturbing and terrifying. Then, when the boys finally catch up to Kenny, who leads them to the cemetery and to his own grave, he shows off his gruesome zombie face and starts dissolving like that guy in "Poltergeist," in excruciatingly disturbing detail, before exploding in a pool of blood.

It's enough to make your skin crawl, but it's not even the scariest scene of the episode. That climax comes in later, while the boys are playing "GTA VI" at Butters' house. We see the zombie Kenny monster with long spiky teeth, deranged eyes and elongated limbs with claws crawling out of the TV like Samara Morgan from "The Ring." It is the stuff of pure nightmares, and by far the scariest scene in 2026 television.

Coros says it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

Sources indicate that this watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

According to recent reports, that price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is presently on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that released earlier this year.

Industry observers note that built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

Previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

It has been revealed that coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:.

Industry observers note that music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

On paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.

  • Recent findings suggest that in this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that marvel Comics fans know Doctor Victor von Doom is scarcely ever seen without his iron mask — a mask that hides his supposedly horribly scarred face. But with Marvel Studios choosing former Tony Stark actor Robert Downey Jr. to play Doom in the upcoming "Avengers" movies "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars," there's been an expectation that Doom's mask coming off will be a jaw dropping moment.

Now, Chris Evans has claimed that Doom wears his mask for the entirety of "Doomsday." But that could only mean he'll keep the mask on until "Secret Wars." Even then, there's the chance that Doom is so disfigured that his face isn't even recognizable as RDJ. A new TV spot for "Doomsday" does suggest Doom has his scarred face, while also teasing we're eventually going to see exactly what's under his mask ... but not yet.

Recent findings suggest that in this TV spot, Magneto (Ian McKellen) tries to telekinetically rip off Doom's mask — it is made of metal, after all. But Doom does not restrict himself to the laws of science. There's evidently a magical seal on the mask (note there appear to be runic designs across Doom's costume), because glowing green tendrils extend out from Doom's hood and grab the mask, slamming it back onto Doom's face. A brief glimpse of Doom's face, visible through the mask's eyeholes, demonstrates hints of pale macerated skin and scar tissue.

In the "Fantastic Four" comics, it was originally noted that Doom suffered his scars during an experiment in college. A machine he built to contact the "nether world" (later revealed to be an attempt to reach his mother's damned soul) exploded in his face, leaving him scarred.

It has been revealed that now, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby intended that Doom actually only had a thin facial scar — but Doom's ego can't stand even that small imperfection. Later "Fantastic Four" writer/artist John Byrne melded the two ideas. The machine explosion only slightly damaged Doom's face, but then Victor — convinced his face was already ruined — put his freshly forged mask on before it cooled, and that is why he has a horribly scarred face.

The greatest source of Doom's torment is completely self-inflicted. The exemplary 1989 "Doctor Strange and Doctor Doom: Triumph and Torment" goes with Byrne's interpretation. When Doom seeks out the wisdom of the wizard named the Aged Genghis, the sorcerer alludes to Doom's "minor disfigurement." We then see Doom's (barely scarred) face as Victor lashes out at the insult.

According to recent reports, it's unclear what origin "Doomsday" will go with, if any of them. Marketing suggests the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Doom will be driven by a lost wife and child, not his mother. What is clear from this TV spot is that Marvel fans can expect to see Doom and Magneto — the two greatest villains of Marvel Comics — clash onscreen. Doom's wizardry here refutes the obvious conclusion that Magneto wins easily because he controls metal and Doom is concealed inside metal armor.

"He is pain, he is extinction," Magneto declares, setting up Doom's famous third person double entendre: "I am Doom!" Ian McKellen's Magneto was the first villain of the Marvel movie boom that kicked off with 2000's "X-Men." Bringing him back to face (and presumably fall to) Doom is some classic carnival barker marketing that would make Stan Lee proud.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is set for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.
