💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dani Kessel Odom (they/them) is an autistic lead writer and TV critic who covers sci-fi demonstrates like Doctor Who and Pluribus, fantasy shows like The Magicians and Percy Jackson, and horror of all kinds.
  • Dani is also part of ScreenRant's books team, using their fiction writing and literature studies as the backbone for their book analyses.
  • They have covered events, such as the Denver Fan Expo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dani Kessel Odom (they/them) is an autistic lead writer and TV critic who covers sci-fi demonstrates like Doctor Who and Pluribus, fantasy shows like The Magicians and Percy Jackson, and horror of all kinds. They also cover Marvel and DC TV shows and movies, with a robust knowledge of comic books. Their TV reviews can be found on Rotten Tomatoes.

Dani is also part of ScreenRant's books team, using their fiction writing and literature studies as the backbone for their book analyses.

They have covered events, such as the Denver Fan Expo. Professionals in the field, such as Damien Leone and Lucy Hale, have shared their articles. Their review of Ponies was quoted in the show's TV trailer.

In university, they majored in English Writing with a minor in psychology. They have always had a passion for analyzing TV and movies, even taking filmography and scriptwriting classes in university. They also studied and participated in onstage and onscreen acting extensively from the ages of 7 to 18.

Aside from working at Screen Rant, Dani has worked as a freelance editor and writer over the past decade, often in a ghostwriting capacity.

Sources indicate that the dystopian sci-fi genre has introduced readers to many terrifying worlds, but these nine stand out for being truly disturbing on another level. Like every sci-fi subgenre, dystopian books' popularity comes in waves, and it tends to grow during times of political and social unrest. The 2010s dystopian YA boom came just two years after the recession. Then, in the year after the 2016 US Presidential election, the BBC reported a 9,500% increase in 1984 sales. They also shared that Brave Upcoming World hit the Top 10 on Amazon and Fahrenheit 451 jumped to 15 on the charts.

According to recent reports, because dystopian novels gain traction based on current events and social anxieties, what resonates with audiences at one time may not have the same effect later. For instance, The Time Machine by H.G. Wells reads more like a campy Victorian adventure book now, even though it was once perceived as a terrifying dystopian story. Similarly, Logan’s Run is still deeply entertaining, but the top-notch sci-fi book and movie adaptation don’t have the same bite as they did when overpopulation was the major matter on everyone’s mind.

It has been revealed that looking at our current world, nine dystopian novels stand out as poignant and terrifying. They have parallels to our current world, or they speak to fears about what could come down the line.

Some dystopian books are upsetting because they are so extreme. Parable of the Sower hits hard because it’s disturbingly realistic. It only feels a step or two ahead of where we are now, with a polarized society ravaged by climate change and governmental failure. Fresh water is hard to come by, and the environment has severely degraded, leading to displacement and rationing of resources.

People live in walled-in communities, protecting themselves with guns. Society has collapsed, leading to high crime rates and rampant substance use disorder. A highly addictive opioid drives folks to commit arson. Because the book feels painfully relevant, it’s extremely difficult to read, but that doesn’t change how crucial the dystopian sci-fi book is.

Purchase Parable of the Sower here.

The Handmaid’s Tale is a cornerstone of the dystopian social sci-fi genre, set in a disturbing world rooted in real-world fear. The theocratic society treats women like objects instead of human beings. They are sorted into hierarchies, including roles like wives, handmaids, and unwomen. Their value is determined solely by the services they can perform for men. Women have no bodily autonomy. They have no individual freedom.

Sources indicate that on top of that, women in Gilead are pitted against each other, reinforcing the system from within and making organized resistance difficult, if not impossible. Unfortunately, the terrifying dystopian world in the book and Hulu adaptation of The Handmaid’s Tale isn’t out of the realm of possibility because religious fundamentalists already legislate female bodies, so the book is more chilling.

Purchase The Handmaid's Tale here.

The Silo book trilogy and Apple TV’s sci-fi show start with an uncomfortable dystopian society formed after an apocalyptic event, but it gets progressively more disturbing as it goes on, eventually ranking up there with the worst of the worst. Each silo has a social class system with three levels. Because they are around 5,760 feet tall, the classes are metaphorically separated and also literally separated, preventing upward mobility.

Then, it gets more disturbing when the books reveal more about the Cleaning in the Silo books. Rather than being affected by nuclear radiation, a nanoterrorist attack caused the toxic air. The founders of the World Order Operation Fifty intentionally released them across the globe.

Purchase the Silo trilogy, including the first book Wool, here.

Industry observers note that ray Bradbury’s masterpiece classic novel, Fahrenheit 451, is downright terrifying because it isn’t just about social problems or governmental control. Instead, the problems run in both directions, creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

Sources indicate that on the one hand, the government in Fahrenheit 451 outlaws books, and they employ the firemen to burn them. They also take steps to sanitize the media. Book banning and censorship are rampant in this world, and that can’t be ignored. On the other hand, the citizens become dangerously complacent, taught to value comfort and entertainment over critical thinking. They’re bombarded with media so much that they don’t have time for silence and personal reflection. There’s no obvious solution, which makes the book chilling.

Nine years before The Hunger Games came out, Koushun Takami released Battle Royale, which has a similar premise. Suzanne Collins has consistently denied any connection (via The New York Times), but the comparison between the two is natural, even if one wasn’t inspired by the other.

While The Hunger Games depicts an awful dystopian society, it pales in comparison to the horrors of Battle Royale’s The Society. In the Japanese story, the young students forced into the battle royale know each other and bring their pre-existing relationships to the island. This makes the deaths feel more personal. On top of that, the violence is chaotic and emotion-driven rather than strategic. There’s also no spectacle in Battle Royale; it eschews glossiness for an unrelenting sense of dread. Ultimately, Battle Royale’s dystopian world lingers long after it ends as nightmare fuel.

Sources indicate that of all the books on this list, 1984 is probably the best-known, given its place on many school curricula. As of 2023, the book had sold over 30 million copies worldwide (via WordsRated), and even folks who haven’t read the book recognize the “Big Brother is watching” phrase. Beyond its popularity, the story also features one of the most disturbing dystopian societies. The ruling party enforces these three slogans:.

Sources indicate that it’s many of the most disturbing dystopian societies wrapped up into one. There’s no thought autonomy, let alone bodily autonomy, and the Party isn’t afraid of brainwashing or disappearing people. What’s more, they use other cult tactics like emotional manipulation with the Two Minutes Hate.

In a recent development, most of the attention Dungeon Crawler Carl gets comes from its absurdist comedy and fever-dream-like story elements. To be fair, those are truly fantastic parts of the book series. However, the story also resonates with audiences because of its disturbing dystopian society, which parallels our own.

Recent findings suggest that the aliens engage in colonialism and commodify human beings (and other species of players). The in-universe showrunners monetize the suffering of others through reality TV. They also manipulate footage to paint Carl in a negative light, manipulating viewers as much as they are the game. On top of all that, the game is designed to create division, and it works. Together, these elements create a truly terrifying dystopian world that feels far enough away to see more objectively, yet close enough to emotionally impact readers.

Purchase Dungeon Crawler Carl here.

It has been revealed that stephen King’s books written under the pen name Richard Bachman are known for being grimmer and more depressing. The Long Walk is especially memorable for its truly awful dystopian world. Stephen King’s story normalizes state-sanctioned cruelty toward teenagers, pitting them in a competition where they must suffer or die.

100 walkers go on a literal death march, knowing that only one competitor will survive. That would already be chilling enough, but the way the rules are enforced is almost worse. They remain completely calm when threatening to murder a teenager, and there’s virtually no remorse for the deaths. It’s almost as if The Long Walk’s world has stripped adults of all humanity, which is a terrifying prospect.

In a recent development, nobel Prize-winning author Kazuo Ishiguro uses speculative fiction to explore existential themes such as collective memory and humanity, and Never Let Me Go is a prime example. That remarked, it’s one of his darkest stories because of its dystopian world, which strips people of their humanity. The entire story rests on the premise that clones are created and live deeply human lives, only to donate vital organs to the point of death.

These beings have memories, emotions, and coming-of-age experiences. They experience love and sadness just like any naturally born individual. Yet society somehow sees them as lesser. Because they're cloned, they aren’t really seen as human. They exist only to die, and it’s emotional to read the story knowing where things are headed for Kathy, Ruth, and Tommy.

In a recent development, prime Video has been serving up a feast for romantic comedy fans in 2026. Lili Reinhart's rom-com "The Love Hypothesis" just finished dominating the Prime Video charts, which came in the wake of Ester Expósito's romantic thriller "Drawn Together" becoming a Prime streaming hit. Now, the streamer has added a Christmas-themed romance just in time for the holidays, and this one stars "Landman" actor Michelle Randolph.

In a recent development, the film is called "Clashing Through the Snow" and before you immediately close this window just let me explain. Yes, the name sounds like the result of a "give me a cheesy Christmas rom-com title" ChatGPT prompt, but Randolph alone should pique your interest. The actor has quietly been delivering standout performances in Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" and his "Yellowstone" prequel "1923." The former sees her play Ainsley Norris, the ditzy but determined daughter of Billy Bob Thornton's oil man Tommy Norris. Based on her performances in those indicates, Randolph surely has a bright future ahead. While "Clashing Through the Snow" might not be her major breakthrough, it's doing pretty darn well on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that until recently, Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale's sports movie "Madden" was topping the Prime Video charts. But it's now been knocked out of the top spot by this festive romance movie, in which publishing editor Hannah Hendricks (Randolph) is forced to take a road trip with her rival, Ryan Mitchell (Chris Briney). You can see where this is going.

According to streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, the film has now hit number two on the United States overall Prime Video chart (which combines TV and films) as of Thanksgiving day, and sits at number one on the movie chart. But Michelle Randolph's comedy is proving popular elsewhere, too. In fact, it's become a global hit. At the time of writing, the film is charting on 61 countries' top 10 movie rankings, which is a pretty good showing. Even more impressive, "Clashing Through the Snow" is number one on the movie charts in 47 of those countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the movie has managed to break into the overall chart in 30 countries, taking the top spot in five of them. That means "Clashing Through the Snow" is the most-watched piece of media on Prime Video in Austria, Poland, Portugal, South Africa, and Switzerland. It even managed to hit number one on the overall chart in the U.S. on November 25, 2026. That's a notable achievement, as often films will break into the top 10 movies without making it onto the overall charts. "Clashing Through the Snow" must be good, then...

It has been revealed that "Clashing Through the Snow" is a comfortingly familiar rom-com outing that's perfect for the holidays. The film sees Chris Briney's Ryan Mitchell and Michelle Randolph's Hannah Hendricks stranded at an airport during a snowstorm, after which they share a rental car and set out on a cross-country trip to New York. The pair both need to close a deal in order to save their jobs — but wouldn't you know it, they fall in love instead. Along the way there's plenty of romantic Christmas movie moments as the couple stop in charming small towns and overcome mishaps together. Is "Clashing Through the Snow" pushing the boundaries of rom-coms? No. Is it charming? Sure is.

The film is directed by Carlson Young, who made her feature directorial debut with the 2021 fantasy horror "The Blazing World" before directing Sophie Turner in 2025's "Trust." She also oversaw a couple of Prime Video rom-coms before "Clashing Through the Snow," directing 2024's "Upgraded" and 2026's "The Last Sunrise.".

According to recent reports, now, she's delivered a major hit with her Randolph-led Christmas rom-com, which has a 77% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. There aren't enough reviews to earn it a critic score yet, but while William Bibbiani of TheWrap found it to be "unapologetically clichéd" he also found the dialogue to be memorable and saw the film as "an efficient delivery mechanism for semi-believable rom and semi-funny com.".

If that sounds appealing, "Clashing Through the Snow" is streaming on Prime Video right now.

#144121. The 10 Best Christmas War Films, Ranked

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Collider ↗ Open Full Page

The 10 Best Christmas War Films, Ranked

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • But while we all celebrate the holidays with our loved ones, we often forget that the world revolves around them.
  • In a recent development, the ten films use Christmas as a backdrop in a variety of ways, yet they all center around the hardships of battle.
  • The epic World War II film Battle of the Bulge dramatizes Nazi Germany’s final major Western Front counteroffensive in the Ardennes forest during the winter of 1944.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘Tis the season to be jolly! But while we all celebrate the holidays with our loved ones, we often forget that the world revolves around them. So, at certain moments in world history, wars broke out during Christmas. What did it mean for the men and women on the battlefield? Well, these ten Christmas war movies may offer some insight!

In a recent development, the ten films use Christmas as a backdrop in a variety of ways, yet they all center around the hardships of battle. From classic films of Hollywood’s Golden Age to newer dramas, these Christmas films may be perfect additions to your holiday rotation. Whether you typically seek out war films or not, the Christmas element may entice you.

The epic World War II film Battle of the Bulge dramatizes Nazi Germany’s final major Western Front counteroffensive in the Ardennes forest during the winter of 1944. As German panzer forces led by Colonel Martin Hessler (Robert Shaw) launch a surprise attack to capture Antwerp, an American intelligence officer named Lieutenant Colonel Daniel Kiley (Henry Fonda) deduces that the advancing enemy tanks will soon run out of fuel and races to stop them from seizing a massive Allied supply depot. Directed by Ken Annakin, Battle of the Bulge works as a holiday film because it presents a Christmas-season WWII setting with a large-scale 1960s roadshow war spectacle known for its tank action sequences, widescreen photography, and strong ensemble cast.

Shot in Ultra Panavision 70 and shown in Cinerama, Battle of the Bulge delivers sweeping armored clashes and memorable set pieces like the tank crews singing "Panzerlied.” Taking historical liberties, the film compresses the campaign and alters terrain and weather, yet presents combat as a heavy, imposing presence. That stated, the Christmas backdrop comes in as the Ardennes offensive ran across the Christmas and Newly introduced Year's holidays in 1944, giving the story a grim seasonal contrast. Benjamin Frankel's score weaves carol motifs, such as "Good King Wenceslas" and "The First Noel,” alongside dramatic battle themes. With stellar star power and poignant human moments trickling in between the battle scenes, the film is an easy marriage of holiday setting and epic war story.

Written and directed by Carl Foreman in a piece he deemed a “personal statement,” The Victors is a gritty, episodic anti-war drama that follows an American infantry squad across Europe during World War II, from Britain and Sicily to France and occupied Berlin. Intercutting fictional vignettes with real wartime newsreels, the film explores the dehumanizing psychological toll of combat and the harsh encounters soldiers share with European civilians, illustrating that war leaves no true winners. While its reception upon release was sharply divided, many contemporary viewers and rediscoveries value its bleak realism, ambitious structure, and early shift toward gritty 1960s filmmaking. Its holiday highlight comes in through a haunting holiday sequence that contrasts festive cheer against the brutal reality of combat.

Adapted from Alexander Baron's The Human Kind, the film was ahead of its time in its darker tone compared with many wartime spectacles of the era. It rejects conventional battle-glorification in favor of moral disillusionment and historical irony. Foreman stages a harrowing firing-squad execution in a snow-covered setting during the holiday season, modeled on the real-life execution of Private Eddie Slovik. It features an ironic holiday soundtrack as Frank Sinatra’s recording of "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas" plays against the grim imagery, sharpening the emotional shock rather than offering warm holiday comfort. Rather than cozy sentimentality, the film highlights the harsh conditions endured by soldiers and civilians, giving viewers a sobering reminder of peacetime comforts during the holidays. With a brilliant ensemble featuring George Peppard, George Hamilton, Eli Wallach, Albert Finney, Peter Fonda, Jeanne Moreau, Melina Mercouri, and Romy Schneider, the anthology-style storytelling is worth experiencing the reality of war. ​​​​​​​.

In the Canadian TV film Silent Night, it loosely tells the true story of German mother named Elisabeth Vincken (Linda Hamilton) and her young son Fritz (Matthew Harbour) as they take refuge in a remote Ardennes forest cabin on Christmas Eve 1944. When three lost American soldiers—one severely wounded—and three German soldiers arrive seeking shelter from the winter storm, Elisabeth convinces both sides to leave their weapons outside and share a peaceful holiday meal. Directed by Rodney Gibbons, Silent Night is a heartfelt retelling of a World War II truce that is grounded in humanity. It turns an intimate Christmas Eve moment and turns it into a character-driven story of hope.

Silent Night is a special film. Rather than relying on large-scale battle spectacle, the intimate cabin setting highlights the contrast between Christmas warmth and war's harshness. Choosing humanity over stereotypes, the soldiers share rations and a holiday meal; initial hostility gives way to shared vulnerability and common ground across enemy lines. Having armed enemies share tight quarters, after agreeing to leave weapons outside, creates genuine suspense and forced empathy. Familiar Christmas traditions like sharing food, trimming a tree, and singing carols collide with grief, fear, and wartime loyalties. Moments of camaraderie stay fragile rather than turning into easy sentimentality. Hamilton stands out, playing Elisabeth with quiet authority and moral clarity, refusing to let hatred or war dictate what happens under her roof. Silent Night takes a true story and does it justice. ​​​​​​​.

While it may not have a direct holiday plotline, Where Eagles Dare gets lumped into the holiday war viewing for its Boxing Day debut and its snow-covered alpine setting. Directed by Brian G. Hutton, the epic action-adventure film set during World War II follows British Major John Smith (Richard Burton) and American Lieutenant Morris Schaffer (Clint Eastwood) as they lead an elite commando unit disguised as German soldiers into the Bavarian Alps to rescue a captured U.S. general holding D-Day invasion plans from an impregnable mountain fortress. As the team infiltrates the castle, they uncover a web of double-crosses and traitors within their own ranks, turning a straightforward rescue into a deadly espionage trap. Where Eagles Dare emerged as a classic, blending high-stakes World War II espionage with relentless, practical action and memorable star power.

In a recent development, written by Alistair MacLean, the story blends a castle-infiltration rescue mission with constant double-crosses and shifting loyalties that keep viewers guessing. Filming on location in Austria and Bavaria, including sequences atop moving cable cars in harsh winter weather, gives the action a visceral weight. With a winter wonderland backdrop, the film receives a fairytale-fortress feel amid blizzards and freezing cold. Burton brings theatrical intensity as Major John Smith while Eastwood plays Lieutenant Morris Schaffer with sharp efficiency. Their pairing creates sharp dramatic friction as the mission escalates. Where Eagles Dare is a sweeping, larger-than-life classic that deserves a watch when a chill fills the air. ​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that directed by Nagisa Ōshima from a screenplay by Ōshima and Paul Mayersberg, the holiday-tinged war film Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence is set in a 1942 Japanese prisoner-of-war camp on Java. The film explores the intense cultural and psychological clash between British captives and their strict Japanese captors during World War II. As rebellious British Major Jack Celliers (David Bowie) sparks a tense battle of wills and mutual fascination with camp commander Captain Yonoi (Ryuichi Sakamoto), fluent Japanese-speaking officer Lt. Col. John Lawrence (Tom Conti) works to bridge their divide and prevent bloodshed. Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence turns a World War II prisoner-of-war story into an intimate psychological study of clashing cultures, honor, and unspoken desire. The film subverts both holiday sentimentality and traditional combat tropes, choosing character over battle.

Sources indicate that merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence explores how rigid military codes and personal guilt shape human connection. Strict Bushido ideals and camp commandant Captain Yonoi's rigid discipline collide with Major Jack Celliers's defiant spirit and Lieutenant Colonel John Lawrence's role as a cultural bridge. Rather than treating captors and prisoners as simple caricatures, the film explores obsession, guilt, and shifting loyalties. Instead of cozy holiday cheer, Christmas arrives amid harsh POW camp conditions, heightening the contrast between seasonal goodwill and wartime cruelty. Its wintry, melancholic mood pairs well with late-year reflection, anchored by themes of forgiveness, memory, and survival. Bowie is absolutely magnetic, bringing distinct intensity and vulnerability. With an emotionally fueled score and its lush, sometimes surreal visuals paired with tense quietness, Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence may not excuse holiday tidings, but it hammers home the power of connection. ​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that one of the greatest war stories ever told is the subject of the Christian Carion film Joyeux Noël. Inspired by the real-life Christmas Truce of 1914, the World War I film follows French, Scottish, and German soldiers on the Western Front who spontaneously lay down their weapons on Christmas Eve to sing carols, share gifts, and play soccer in No Man's Land. As opposing troops bond over their shared humanity, they must eventually confront the harsh disapproval of their military superiors once the fleeting ceasefire ends. Joyeux Noël is a remarkable piece for its emotional impact, international ensemble cast, and poignant depiction of Christmas on the Western Front.

Earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film, Joyeux Noël is a joyous production. Told through multi-language realism, the film reinforces the cross-border camaraderie and cultural friction of the front lines. Joyeux Noël pairs the brutality of World War I trench warfare with the genuine warmth, music, and shared humanity. Music plays a central role, as a Scottish bagpiper and a German opera tenor help spark the ceasefire with familiar holiday songs like "Silent Night" and "Adeste Fideles," turning the battlefield into common ground. Paired with Philippe Rombi's score and snowy winter cinematography, the film sparks the holiday spirit with goodwill front and center. It’s a greeting card-quality film. Rather than ending on a purely fairy-tale note, the story shows the harsh military repercussions soldiers face afterward for fraternizing with the enemy. ​​​​​​​.

In this depiction of the Battle of the Bulge, Battleground director William A. Wellman tells the story of a squad of U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division trapped by German forces in Bastogne, Belgium, during the December 1944 Battle of the Bulge. Cut off from supplies and air support by thick winter fog, the exhausted men battle freezing temperatures, dwindling rations, and disguised enemy infiltrators as they fight to survive until Allied reinforcements can break the siege. The Academy Award-winning war film strips away wartime heroics and grand speeches to show the gritty, everyday reality of American soldiers trapped in Bastogne during the Battle of the Bulge. The film pairs a snowy winter atmosphere and a Christmas Eve service with a grounded portrait of endurance and camaraderie.

It has been revealed that instead of turning the men of the 101st Airborne into larger-than-life icons, screenwriter Robert Pirosh, a veteran of the battle, focuses on fear, fatigue, griping, and moments of doubt. Characters complain, slack off, or briefly consider running away, making their eventual endurance and camaraderie feel earned rather than inevitable. The film relies on an ensemble cast, including Van Johnson, John Hodiak, Ricardo Montalbán, George Murphy, and Oscar-nominated James Whitmore, working as a unit rather than centering on a single star. Christmas Eve in the line serves as a monumental moment in the film. A chaplain holds a Christmas service for the men, framing why the fight against fascism is necessary while soldiers face overwhelming odds and German surrender demands. Once the weather clears enough for planes to reach the trapped troops, supply drops of food, fuel, and ammunition act like hard-won holiday gifts. Battleground is an unvarnished story with dark humor, stark black-and-white winter visuals, and genuine realism. ​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that set in snowy Ardennes Forest in December 1944, A Midnight Clear, written and directed by Keith Gordon, follows a depleted six-man American intelligence squad stationed at an isolated French chateau as they encounter a weary German platoon that wants to surrender rather than fight in Germany's final offensive. After sharing an unexpected Christmas truce with their enemies, the young soldiers arrange a staged skirmish, so the Germans can safely surrender without being branded traitors, only for a tragic misunderstanding to turn their peaceful plan deadly. A Midnight Clear trades typical combat action for a quiet, character-driven study of isolation, morality, and absurdity during World War II. Adapted from William Wharton's novel, the film stands out as a great Christmas film, using the holiday's quiet, reflective spirit to capture the grim emotional toll of World War II.

Recent findings suggest that christmas carols, a makeshift tree, and a snowball fight contrast sharply with winter cold, psychological weight, and the grim realities of conflict. Snow-covered woods, isolated estates, and eerie quiet give the film a fairy-tale, almost surreal tone. Despite the war backdrop, the winter setting underscores isolation and fragility. The film refuses easy sentimentality. Its tragic turn reminds viewers how fragile peace is when war's machinery is still running. The film features strong, grounded performances from Ethan Hawke, Gary Sinise, Kevin Dillon, Arye Gross, Peter Berg, Frank Whaley, and John C. McGinley. Rather than relying on grand heroics, the cast captures young men dealing with fear, fatigue, and unspoken strain. A Midnight Clear has the DNA of a war saga, but its haunting winter atmosphere turns it into something grander. ​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that directed by John Cromwell, the 1944 war epic Since You Went Away follows Anne Hilton (Claudette Colbert) and her two daughters, Jane and Bridget (Jennifer Jones and Shirley Temple), as they navigate rationing, romance, and personal sacrifices on the American home front after her husband leaves for World War II. Joined by a retired colonel and loyal household staff, the family endures wartime heartbreak and uncertainty before receiving hopeful news on Christmas Eve. Since You Went Away is a moving portrayal of World War II home-front life. With a deeply emotional Christmas Eve payoff, Since You Went Away is a perfect Yuletide classic to share with the family.

Industry observers note that unlike war films centered on combat, this home-front classic focuses on individuals as they navigate rationing, separation, and everyday worries at home. It captures the longing, resilience, and hope of families waiting for loved ones to return that resonates with a timeless sentiment for any wartime family. Rather than focusing on the battlefield, the emotional power stems from daily life in America, where ration books, victory gardens, housing shortages, scrap drives, and civilian sacrifice were a reality. The story balances lighthearted moments, like a hangar dance and teenage romance, with gut-wrenching goodbyes, including Jane and Bill Smollett’s (Robert Walker) famous midnight train station parting. Since You Went Away may be the most sentimental Christmas-based war film of all time. ​​​​​​​.

Blending dark comedy and suspenseful mystery inside a World War II prisoner-of-war camp, Stalag 17 is a brilliant feature. Directed by Billy Wilder, the story follows barracks of American airmen who suspect a cynical, black-marketeering sergeant named J.J. Sefton (William Holden) of being a Nazi informant after two escaping prisoners are killed. Determined to clear his name, Sefton investigates the barracks to expose the real German spy and orchestrate a daring escape. Stalag 17 balances broad barracks humor and gallows comedy with genuine paranoia and suspense as American airmen hunt for a German spy among them. Set during Christmas week in 1944, the holiday becomes a source of brilliant irony.

In a recent development, between Wilder's direction and Holden's Oscar-winning lead performance, Stalag 17 is simply wonderful. The tension comes from paranoia inside Barracks 4 as American airmen try to figure out who is leaking escape plans. The film builds suspense to an epic reveal set to "When Johnny Comes Marching Home,” earning it an iconic moment in the genre and a blueprint for directing tension. As for the Christmas backdrop, makeshift decorations, dog-tag trees, and a camp Christmas party clash with the harsh reality of captivity and fatal escape attempts. Camp commandant Colonel von Scherbach (Otto Preminger) even plays a cruel parody of holiday generosity around an inspection. The film celebrates bittersweet camaraderie in moments like when the men dance together during the holiday celebration and Stanislas "Animal" Kuzawa’s (Robert Strauss) poignant mix of slapstick and loneliness. They highlight brotherhood and longing for home without turning overtly sentimental. Adapted from the Broadway play by former POWs Donald Bevan and Edmund Trzcinski, the film treats captivity with a realistic edge rather than pure escapism. It even shaped later television comedies like Hogan's Heroes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, unveiled on Wednesday, November 25 the final additions to the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

In a recent development, the newly confirmed honorees include “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and costume designer Trish Summerville, who will be receiving the Spotlight Award. They join previously announced honorees John Turturro, Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield, Ike Barinholtz, Yura Borisov, James Gray, Adam Driver, Beth de Araújo, Mason Reeves, Gemma Chan, Ruth Madeley, David Greaves, Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo, Jeon Do-yeon, Anthony Ippolito, James Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, Mag Sarnowska, Paul Lambert, and Travis Knight. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

Industry observers note that additionally, IndieWire has announced that the incoming awards ceremony will be hosted by writer and comedian Demi Adejuyigbe, whose latest special “Demi Adejuyigbe Is Going to Do 1 (One) Backflip” is now available to stream on Dropout. Previous IndieWire Honors emcees include Emmy winner Alex Edelman, Emmy nominee Robby Hoffman, multi-hyphenate Dewayne Perkins, and lauded comedians Vinny Thomas and Atsuko Okatsuka.

IndieWire Honors will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well.

It has been revealed that “It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”.

Industry observers note that “It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” remarked James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”.

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:.

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most crucial women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for newly introduced talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for latest distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she noted uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

Recent findings suggest that there is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she notes. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Industry observers note that madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

It has been revealed that as the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

Though the latest film from director David Fincher and screenwriter Quentin Tarantino furthers the mis-adventures of Cliff Booth, the role that earned star Brad Pitt an Oscar, the Netflix film has an identity all its own. The work of costume designer Trish Summerville and actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II are two elements that put that into focus, really easing the audience into the jump forward to 1977, where the silks flowed, and fur dripped off new screen icons akin to the latter’s Rodrick “Hot Rod” Harrison. This go-round allows viewers to have an appreciation for more than just Hollywood, but the greater Los Angeles area, and all the distinct styles it brought in that pivotal ‘70s moment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

Writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

Sources indicate that executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

It has been revealed that indieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”.

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

Recent findings suggest that “No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”.

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he remarked, that was never really on his radar.

Sources indicate that “When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” said Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”.

The process was a “very challenging one,” he noted, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he stated. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really big influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”.

He added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”.

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

In a recent development, “In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he said. But challenges in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel stated of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.).

In a recent development, “Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he noted.).

Industry observers note that “When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”.

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

Hopefully, more masks and other content, including the long-awaited Master Quest DLC, will also be released soon. According to recent reports, lade Omotade is a News and Features Author at Collider, covering everything from casting announcements and streaming trends to behind-the-scenes stories and the cultural impact of today's biggest film and TV franchises. Since joining the team in 2024, she has written more than 1,000 news stories, with her work also cited by outlets like AOL and IMDb.

Sources indicate that bringing one of literature's greatest works to life is no easy task, but Netflix is rising to the challenge with Pride and Prejudice. Written by Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice was her third novel and the second to be published, released in 1813. At the center is the dynamic between Elizabeth Bennet (whose personal growth drives the story) and the proud, wealthy Mr. Darcy. Through their time together, Elizabeth recognizes the mistakes of judging people too quickly and learns how to distinguish fake charm from true kindness.

Recent findings suggest that in the century since Pride and Prejudice was published, it has been adapted for the screen several times, beginning with a 1938 BBC television broadcast written and directed by Michael Barry. Unfortunately, that version is permanently lost because it aired live before television recording technology existed. Memorable adaptations include the Academy Award-winning movie starring Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier, partly based on Helen Jerome's 1935 stage adaptation; Joe Wright's acclaimed 2005 feature starring Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen; andthe 1995 BBC miniseries starring Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle. Now, the upcoming Netflix version joins the bunch, premiering in just one week.

Starring Emma Corrin and Jack Lowden as Elizabeth and Darcy, Netflix's Pride and Prejudice series was first reported to be in development in October 2024 and officially revealed in April 2025. Filming began in the UK in the summer of 2025, with first-look behind-the-scenes images released in July. Bestselling author and screenwriter Dolly Alderton wrote the series, and Euros Lyn directed. The six-part series premieres on December 3, 2026, as Alderton announced at the Jane Austen Festival in September.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

In a recent development, you do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

In a recent development, you want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

In a recent development, the intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Recent findings suggest that in Netflix's Pride and Prejudice, viewers are treated to a fresh yet faithful adaptation. Elizabeth, the second of five daughters, faces pressure to marry well or risk losing the comfortable life she knows. As she steps into society, she meets the prickly Mr. Darcy, and their love story unfolds alongside that of her older sister Jane, who falls for the charming Mr. Bingley.

Other stars in the Regency romance adaptation include Olivia Colman as the Bennet family matriarch, Mrs. Bennet; Rufus Sewell as her husband, Mr. Bennet; Freya Mavor as the eldest Bennet daughter, Jane; and Rhea Norwood as Lydia Bennet. Newcomers Hollie Avery and Hopey Parish make their debut roles as Kitty and Mary Bennet, respectively. Daryl McCormack will portray Jane's love interest, Mr. Bingley, while Siena Kelly will play his sister, Caroline Bingley.

Netflix's Pride and Prejudice premieres in one week.

  • Recent findings suggest that “To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

Recent findings suggest that “To make them look real, talking about practical and how important that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page said. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”.

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

Sources indicate that “We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”.

Recent findings suggest that cheat codes have long been a part of the Grand Theft Auto video game franchise, and the tradition continues with GTA 6. Not only does GTA 6 support cheats, but it also has a menu that lists all of them as well as instructions for unlocking them. However, you cannot fire up the game and start using cheats from the beginning. In fact, it requires quite a bit of work on your part. Here's how to unlock cheat codes in GTA 6, how to see the list of cheats, as well as the 10 best cheat codes in GTA 6.

Gone are the good old days when you could fire up GTA, enable god mode, unlimited ammo, no reload, spawn a jetpack, and run around the entire city destroying things at will. In GTA 6, you'll need to complete the main story to unlock the ability to use cheat codes. On top of that, you'll have to complete challenges of various difficulty levels to access specific cheat codes. Some of these cheats unlock the moment you finish the main story. Others, however, are quite challenging or time-consuming. For instance, unlimited reload requires you to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges.

Once you complete the main story in GTA 6, just go to in-game settings, and you'll see a fresh Cheats tab. This lists all 61 cheats and how to unlock them. You'll see the actual button combo for each cheat right after you complete the unlock requirement.

Unfortunately, there are some serious gameplay ramifications to using cheat codes in GTA 6. For starters, you can't save the game once you input even one cheat code. That's why it's best to save before you start using cheats, to avoid losing progress. Using cheat codes will also disable trophies and achievements in GTA 6.

To start using cheat codes in GTA 6, you'll have to get your character to pull up the smartphone by pressing the up arrow on the D-Pad. Then, hold L1+R1, and press the cheat's key combination on the D-Pad.

While there are a lot of cheat codes in GTA 6, these are 10 of the best, listed with the right key combination, and the condition to unlock them:.

Lose a three-star wanted level 50 times to unlock this cheat. The key combination is left, down, right, down, up, right, up.

This cheat unlocks the moment you wrap up the main story. Press this to unlock: down, up, up, down, up, down, up, down, up, right.

Industry observers note that this is the third cheat that unlocks when you finish the main story. When you shoot or punch/kick characters, this cheat will launch them in the air. The key combination is: down, up, left, right, down, down, up, down.

Sources indicate that if you win 25 silver medals at shooting ranges, you can unlock infinite ammo in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, down.

To stop needing reloads, you need to win 25 gold medals at shooting ranges in GTA 6. The key combination is: down, up, right, down, left, left, up, down, down, up.

Sources indicate that if you complete 100 workouts during your GTA 6 playthrough, you'll unlock the cheat that lets you instantly obtain body armor. Press this key combination to make it work: down, up, left, up, up, up, up, up, down, down.

‘All of a Sudden’: Why Does an 11-Minute Scene Centered on a Whiteboard Lecture Work So Well Onscreen?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it is an unorthodox sequence.
  • Recent findings suggest that while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients.
  • In a recent development, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it is an unorthodox sequence. In the middle of “All of a Sudden,” Mari (Tao Okamoto) pulls out a whiteboard and markers to diagram the principles of nature vs. capitalism for her fresh friend Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira). The scene lasts 11 minutes and digs into material you would expect in a university seminar, not the latest cinematic achievement from the Oscar-winning director of “Drive My Car,” Ryūsuke Hamaguchi.

Recent findings suggest that while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Hamaguchi acknowledged the whiteboard is not what we generally consider to be cinematic, but then again neither is the three-hour-and-17-minute film about two women who form a powerful bond by talking about life, their life’s work, and the ever so sexy topic of eldercare for dementia patients. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

In a recent development, and yet “All of a Sudden” blew away the world’s toughest critics at Cannes. Now, its distributor, Neon, heads into this weekend’s holiday theatrical release believing it has a legit shot at winning over the more commercially oriented Oscar voters — and becoming one of the (increasingly common) foreign-language Best Picture nominations. Neon similarly released “Sentimental Value” and “The Secret Agent” to Best Picture nominations the year before.

The whiteboard scene is not an extraneous aside, but a critical turning point in the women’s relationship. We asked the film’s writer/director why it not only works, but was deemed vital to the film.

“In trying to answer why this somehow works, I think there’s a few layers to it,” noted Hamaguchi while on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “And one maybe is because it really is something that is far removed from what is generally considered as cinematic. Perhaps because of that, it brings about a certain suspense, where you wonder, ‘OK, what is this for? What is this actually going to do?’ And there’s a certain sense of wondering that happens.”.

The scene comes a little over an hour into the film. Neither woman wants their magical evening to end. Mari follows Marie-Lou to her job as director of a nursing home, where she struggles to implement her passion project, “Huminitude,” a patient-centered care method based on touch and eye contact, which Mari sees in action. What prompts Mari’s whiteboard seminar is an attempt to help her latest companion put into perspective the resistance she faces in implementing Huminitude and open the door to problem-solving.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the second part [of why the scene works] really comes down to the efforts of the actors that are performing this scene,” mentioned Hamaguchi of Okamoto and Efira, who shared the Best Actress Prize at Cannes. “For Tao, I think it was an incredibly difficult scene to perform because first of all she really needed to understand all of the concepts that she was describing here and to really understand everything intellectually. And so in her preparation she did read a lot of the relevant books to really understand what she is talking about.”.

Recent findings suggest that hamaguchi believes the key to his dialogue-driven film is not necessarily how the words are spoken, but the performance of the listening and how the words are received. In Efira’s whiteboard scene, we see a shift from determined frustration to open enthusiasm that changes the direction of the film itself.

“The attitude of listening that Virginie portrays in this moment, I think, is very notable and really supports this scene,” mentioned Hamaguchi. “She’s not uninterested in what is going on, but in fact she feels that this is something that she should really be exploring together and she’s there and very much present. And I think this attitude of interest and curiosity really starts to work on the audience as well. And so in that sense I think ultimately this scene really works because of the actors’ performances.”.

It has been revealed that one topic that comes up in most post-screening Q&As is that both actresses were not working in the native language. Hamaguchi himself had to work with an interpreter to direct his leads. This is not the first time Hamaguchi has worked this way. On the podcast, he said that, in his experience directing the play inside “Drive My Car,” the language barrier was less of a hindrance and could even aid actors in listening to one another, as shown in the whiteboard scene.

According to recent reports, “I felt that, in fact, this kind of difficulty that exists can in fact provide an environment for even more heightened concentration than you might have if you were speaking the same language,” noted Hamaguchi. “ I think that actually when you can actually hear a lot and get a lot of information from somebody’s voice, you can, in fact, precisely feel just how concentrated the person is when they’re saying something by listening to their voice.”.

Asked if any of his collaborators or producers ever questioned the whiteboard scene after reading the script, Hamaguchi said no, and speculated why: “Because it’s so unusual, I think people understood that this is something that I really wanted to do.”.

“There were some questions around, ‘This section feels a little long. Is there anything we can do about that?’” recalled Hamaguchi, adding that he made a concerted effort to cut his four-hour script to a three-hour, 16-minute running time.

Recent findings suggest that “For me, I was ultimately trying to bring in the shortest version that I felt was accurate for this moment. But ultimately, there is this understanding that this moment is a very important turning point within the film, and so I believe that the producers also understood this.”.

“All of a Sudden” is now playing in select theaters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magneto's biggest costume redesign is coming to the X-Men's fresh reboot, with an older Master of Magnetism donning the suit to fight entire armies. All Magneto truly needs to be instantly recognized anywhere in pop culture is his signature helmet and a flowing cape. Functionally, the horn-rimmed helmet shields Max Eisenhardt’s mind from Charles Xavier’s telepathy, but visually, it crowns him like a defiant warrior-king who refuses to bow to human authority. Magneto's cape billows dramatically whenever he hovers through the air on magnetic fields, signaling his status as mutantkind’s self-appointed sovereign and protector.

Marvel artists have reinvented Magneto’s wardrobe for more than six decades of X-Men comics. His classic 1963 crimson-and-violet uniform established his bold appearance before later eras introduced latest designs. Magneto wore his sleeveless purple-and-magenta trial jumpsuit during Chris Claremont’s Uncanny X-Men #200, and his battle-worn armor with flowing silver hair in Age of Apocalypse. Later on, Cullen Bunn’s Uncanny X-Men run introduced an armored black-and-red revolutionary suit, and the Ultimate Universe put an elegant spin on Magneto's classic costume with a simple combination of a red suit, a black cape, and a black helmet.

Magneto's costumes tend to be so beautifully designed that one arc or series is never enough to do them justice.

According to recent reports, R.B. Silva's Midnight X-Men concept art previously revealed a more traditional-looking costume design for the Midnight Universe's Magneto, sporting a dark purple helmet and an elegant coat covering a sharp combo of dark vest and dark pants. However, Declan Shalvey's variant cover for Midnight X-Men #4 reveals a very different costume. Magneto is depicted using his powers to annihilate an entire vampire army, his sleeveless white Marvel NOW! suit shining bright, with a large white cape flowing in the wind as he descends from the sky with his arms spread out.

In a universe where mutants and humans wage a war for survival against a vampire horde, Midnight X-Men's Magneto acts as a cleansing force against the undead plague, flanked by fellow mutants like Scarlet Witch and Quicksilver. Magneto's decision to wear a gleaming white suit instead of his classic crimson-and-violet war colors reinforces his purifying mission in this timeline. Although he tends to abandon his extremist methods gradually with every shared threat he faces alongside the X-Men all across the Marvel multiverse, Midnight X-Men's version of Magneto has moved past conquering humanity to become mutantkind's shining shield quite prematurely.

After seven live-action movies from X-Men to Dark Phoenix, both Ian McKellen and Michael Fassbender wore several variations of Magneto’s classic red-and-purple armor or dark trench coats, never once suiting up in anything resembling the striking white-and-chrome ensemble made famous in Jonathan Hickman’s late-2010s House of X. Besides translating the gleaming white suit to the big screen for the very first time, and besides honoring one of Magneto's most celebrated comic-book designs of the modern era, Marvel could signal a new era for Magneto's stories on the big screen where none of his previous movie arcs are repeated.

Fox's X-Men movies spent several installments and multiple timeline resets on Erik Lehnsherr’s slow transformation into a mutant extremist and back into a reluctant anti-hero, and Avengers: Doomsday adds Ian McKellen's Magneto to the X-Men's lineup as a seasoned and fully heroic member. The MCU's X-Men reboot can skip repetitive villain origin beats and align Magneto with Charles Xavier and the X-Men far sooner and symbolize his genuine intentions to be a hero with an all-white costume that mirrors his Krakoan heroism. In fact, considering Marvel Studios may explore everything Fox didn't cover, Magneto's white costume could easily debut in a direct Krakoan-era movie.

What's your favorite Magneto look?

Midnight X-Men #4 is now available from Marvel Comics.
