Latest Update: 7 Sci-Fi Books That Are Better Than 'Neuromancer'

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, cyberpunk wouldn't be what it is today without Neuromancer.
  • However, Neuromancer can be a difficult and disorienting read for some.
  • Set in a dystopian 21st century, Snow Crash depicts a Los Angeles that is vividly different, one where corporations rule and governments falter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, cyberpunk wouldn't be what it is today without Neuromancer. Long before computers and the Internet became part of everyday life, sci-fi writers were already imagining what the world might look like with such technology, but more importantly, how it would affect humanity. Neuromancer is one of those books, imagining a dystopian society controlled by global computer networks and introducing hackers like Case, who push the boundaries of artificial intelligence.

However, Neuromancer can be a difficult and disorienting read for some. While it's an essential part of the genre, other books explore similar ideas in ways that some readers might find more engaging. From a cyberpunk reimagining of an American classic to stories about mind-controlling viruses, here are sci-fi books that are better than Neuromancer.

Set in a dystopian 21st century, Snow Crash depicts a Los Angeles that is vividly different, one where corporations rule and governments falter. By day, Hiro Protagonist is a Mafia pizza delivery driver. By night, he's a freelance hacker. When a mysterious digital drug called Snow Crash causes a fellow hacker to suffer brain damage, Hiro gets to the bottom of it—only to discover a sinister conspiracy that could endanger not only the lives of Angelians, but the entire world.

Casual sci-fi fans who find Neuromancer a tough read may prefer Snow Crash. Neal Stephenson's novel is more accessible and entertaining than Gibson's noir-inspired classic, but still offers plenty of investigative intrigue. Its cyberspace is also easier to picture, with virtual worlds, customizable avatars, and interconnected networks that feel familiar today. Published over three decades ago, Snow Crash remains relevant, especially in its depiction of a world where corporations control entire territories.

According to recent reports, forget F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby—K.M. Fajardo gives the American classic a cyberspace twist in Local Heavens. The year is 2075, and Filipino-American Nick Carraway has moved to New York City, now dubbed the Fractured New Americas. Towering skyscrapers loom over the city, while the slums of the working middle class lie beneath them. But despite cynicism over capitalism, Nick can't help but be charmed by the charismatic new-money Jay Gatsby.

According to recent reports, bringing hacking into a familiar tale of admiration, love, and jealousy might seem like an odd choice, but Local Heavens makes it work by giving Nick's mission a personal angle. Unlike Neuromancer, where hacking serves a larger heist, it becomes a source of emotional conflict here. Nick is a corporate-sanctioned hacker assigned to investigate Jay, but the deeper he gets into Jay's world of wealthy people using technology to cheat death, the more he finds himself drawn to Jay, putting his mission at risk.

In a recent development, in The Shockwave Rider, America has become a dystopia where government agencies and corporations have near-total control over computer networks. Not everyone is willing to play along, especially Nick Haflinger, a gifted programmer on the run from Tarnover, a secret program that trained him to serve the state. Armed with a stolen access code, he manipulates the network to stay one step ahead of his pursuers. But one wrong move could expose him and put him right back in their hands.

According to recent reports, for a novel published more than half a century ago, it's mind-blowing how prophetic The Shockwave Rider is, especially since the internet was still in its infancy. While Neuromancer imagines cyberspace as a high-concept medium accessible only through neural interfaces, The Shockwave Rider reveals how cyberspace is much closer to our personal lives, with computer networks connecting homes, offices, and public terminals. It also offers a sharper look at surveillance culture, showing how easily institutions can access and exploit our personal data.

If you've watched the Blade Runner movies, it's imperative that you read the original novel it's based on. Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? is set on a post-apocalyptic Earth where radioactive fallout has driven most animals to extinction. Rick Deckard, a San Francisco bounty hunter, hopes to earn enough money to replace his electric sheep by hunting six rogue androids that have escaped from Mars.

People often talk about artificial intelligence as if artificial beings are nothing more than machines. While that may be true in a technical sense, Dick challenges this assumption by exploring the philosophical implications of AI rather than just its mechanics. He questions whether artificial beings deserve the same empathy, freedom, and dignity as humans, especially when supposedly empathetic people demonstrate cruelty and indifference toward other living beings. As AI becomes increasingly humanlike, Dick's questions about what separates humans from machines feel more relevant than ever.

Industry observers note that nobody is safe in Gnomon. In an alternate, futuristic Britain, an all-seeing AI keeps the population under constant surveillance. Government investigator Mielikki Neith is assigned to investigate the death of Diana Hunter, who died during a forced extraction of her memories. But as Neith examines Hunter's recorded thoughts, she uncovers something far more disturbing than a suspicious death: a hidden danger that could expose the surveillance system's nature and threaten the society built around it.

Gnomon may not share Neuromancer's cyberspace premise, but it offers a different, equally unsettling vision of technological control. When technology becomes the infrastructure of an entire society, surveillance extends beyond tracking people's physical movements to probing their thoughts and memories. Nick Harkaway's novel raises urgent questions about privacy and consent for ordinary people, concerns that feel especially timely in an internet age when personal data is constantly collected, stored, and exposed without people's knowledge or permission.

Recent findings suggest that in a technologically advanced future, artificial intelligence has evolved beyond human comprehension in Void Star. Only a select few can interpret its thoughts, making them valuable assets. Told from three perspectives, the novel follows Irina, a corporate consultant who translates AI-generated thoughts; Thales, the son of a Brazilian politician; and Kern, a streetwise thief raised in the favelas. Their lives collide when Irina and Thales discover that someone can remotely extract memories stored in their cranial implants.

Zachary Mason's Void Star is essentially Neuromancer for readers who want cyberpunk that feels closer to the world we live in today. Building on the ideas established by Gibson, the novel brings them into a future shaped by climate change, mass displacement, autonomous weapons, and extreme wealth inequality. Although the story follows three main characters, the shifting perspectives are easy to follow and add nuance by showing how each experiences the same technological and social problems.

Industry observers note that death is no longer an glitch in Altered Carbon. Set 350 years in the future, Richard K. Morgan's novel imagines a world where cortical stacks implanted in people's spines store their consciousness, allowing them to transfer into upcoming bodies called sleeves. But immortality doesn’t come cheap. The wealthy can afford replacement bodies and backups, while poorer people still risk dying for good. In this world, staying alive even depends on how much money you have.

Industry observers note that while Neuromancer explores cyberspace, corporate AI, and crime through an investigative plot, Altered Carbon brings those technological anxieties into the human body. Its technology can preserve consciousness, but it can't resolve the moral questions that come with it, from bodily ownership to the privilege of living forever. Morgan takes Neuromancer's criticism of capitalism and makes it more personal, turning it into a dilemma about bodily autonomy and how far people are willing to go to preserve their lives.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5.
  • Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers.
  • You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a fresh, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "presently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a latest unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

In a recent development, if you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Sources indicate that amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

In a recent development, there are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a latest console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:.

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

In a recent development, by far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The Hawk,” a Will Ferrell golf comedy that debuted just this summer, has been canceled by Netflix and will not return for a second season, an individual with knowledge told IndieWire.

Ferrell co-created the series in which he plays a former top golfer who is now trying to return to the tour. And while it figured to be a tentpole series for Netflix, one that carried possibly the most expensive budget for a comedy series on Netflix and reunited Ferrell with his “SNL” co-star Molly Shannon and co-creator Harper Steele, it didn’t connect with critics or audiences.

“The Hawk” spent just three weeks on Netflix’s Top 10 when it debuted back in July, topping out at #2 in its second week on Netflix with just 6.2 million views. Ferrell’s vulgar, loudly-dressed golfer with a personalized visor and major mess of bleached blonde hair played a lot like some of Ferrell’s other string of sports comedies throughout the years. But even our critic was perplexed by the series’ tone that makes it sometimes play like a “bizarre addiction drama.” Related Stories ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down.

Steele, in a recent appearance on “Late Night with Seth Meyers,” tipped her hand a little that the show was likely ending when she let slip that, “I was working on a short-lived but probably the best show ever, ‘The Hawk.’”.

The cancellation comes in the wake of a changing of the guard at Netflix, with Peter Rice taking over for veteran creative chief Bela Bajaria. Our critic also recently wrote about the challenges Netflix is facing right now in getting audiences to discover new series in the ways they used to.

But at the same time, Netflix has already renewed a couple of other comedy series that even premiered after “The Hawk” later this year, including “Nobody Wants This,” “A Different World,” “Tires,” “Big Mistakes,” and “The Four Seasons.” Netflix is also still working with Ferrell’s Gloria Sanchez Productions on three latest series, “All the Rage,” “Prep,” and another scripted series from Nikki Glaser.

Deadline first reported the news.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.
  • Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

According to recent reports, in Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, Newly introduced Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

In a recent development, and in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

It has been revealed that there are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

  • Taking over One Piece's Sunday slot on Fuji TV, this 19-episode remake has been on a roll since its October premiere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after years of pure torture in Earth's Hell, trapped in a cocoon surrounded by singing fairies and dancing angels, Frieza is finally back in Dragon Ball Super: Beerus. The enhanced remake spent its first six episodes tightening up the God of Destruction Beerus saga, but episode #7, “Resurrection 'F',” brought the Emperor of the Universe back into the picture. Sorbet and Tagoma used Earth's Dragon Balls to revive him, and now episode #8 is ready to kick the Golden Frieza saga into full gear.

Recent findings suggest that that makes this a significant test for Toei Animation. The original Dragon Ball Super TV retelling of Resurrection 'F' became infamous in 2015 for its rushed schedule, something that even the creator, Akira Toriyama, was unhappy about. Frieza's return deserves a lot better, especially after the remake has spent weeks showing just how much the studio can improve the old material.

Taking over One Piece's Sunday slot on Fuji TV, this 19-episode remake has been on a roll since its October premiere. Toei trimmed the original 14-episode Beerus arc down to six tight installments, cutting out dragged-out fights and overblown gags while giving the visuals a major facelift. If episode #8 keeps that same energy going through Frieza's comeback, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus could set the stage perfectly for the upcoming Dragon Ball Super: The Galactic Patrol anime, which will adapt the Moro arc.

It has been revealed that dragon Ball Super: Beerus episode #8, titled “Revenge 'F',” officially premieres on Sunday, November 29, 2026, at 8:00 AM PST / 11:00 AM EST (4:00 PM GMT) on Crunchyroll and Hulu. It will also be accessible through Disney+. Meanwhile, Netflix viewers in the US will have to wait a little longer, as episode #8 won’t arrive on the platform until Saturday, December 5, making it a six-day delay.

Australian Eastern Daylight Time (AEDT).

The English dub is also underway on Crunchyroll, with Sean Schemmel and Christopher R. Sabat back as Goku and Vegeta. Dubbed episodes aren’t released simultaneously with the Japanese version, though. Newly introduced episodes drop on Thursdays at 8:00 AM PT, and the dub is currently running roughly five episodes behind Japan after launching on November 12.

In a recent development, now that Frieza has been pieced back together aboard Sorbet’s ship, it’s time for the tyrant to get back to work. Episode #8 moves into his infamous four-month training run, the one that leads to his Golden form. Meanwhile, Goku and Vegeta are training under Whis on Beerus’s planet, working toward Super Saiyan Blue. With Toei Animation keeping this 19-episode remake moving at a much snappier pace, there’s little reason to expect the studio to spend too long getting Frieza and his 1,000-soldier army to Earth.

It has been revealed that the episode is also expected to close on a hype note, with Gohan, Piccolo, and the rest of the Z Fighters holding the line while they wait for Goku and Vegeta. That’s a familiar setup, but Resurrection 'F' has a decade of baggage to deal with. The original story drew plenty of criticism for its messy power scaling, and tracksuit Gohan remains one of the saga’s most infamous choices. Cleaner animation is a welcome start, but Toei needs tighter storytelling to make this return land.

After wrapping up the God of Destruction Beerus saga in just six episodes, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus isn’t slowing down for Frieza’s comeback. With the remake reportedly set for 19 episodes covering the Beerus, Golden Frieza, and Universe 6 sagas, the Resurrection 'F' retelling could be done in just six or seven more. That would leave room for Champa’s tournament, while cutting a lot of fat from the 2015 anime, which spent 13 episodes on Frieza’s return alone and more than 40 on all three arcs.

Industry observers note that the story may be familiar from the movie and the original TV anime, but this remake is giving it a fresh shot. Toei’s tighter pacing and reworked visuals are already making a difference. Now episode #8 has to keep that momentum going, because Frieza’s return deserves more than a prettier rerun. If the remake can stick the landing here, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus might finally deliver the sharp opening run this series should have had from the start.

According to recent reports, one of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo. Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo, as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

Apple will also introduce fresh colors on the MacBook Neo “frequently,” though it’s unclear if we’ll see that with the next iteration. From the Power On newsletter:.

Industry observers note that the other thing I’ve heard is that Apple intends to refresh the MacBook Neo’s colors frequently. We’ll see if that trend starts with the first follow-up.

I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo, especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

The bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Hopefully backlit keyboard if they increase price.

Apple increased the price of MacBook Neo from $599 to $699 back in June, and in October the company also silently decreased the education discount by $50, meaning the education price has increased from $499 to $649 since launch.

If there is a price increase, it likely won’t be too major, maybe $50 – leaving the computer at $749. Compared to the rest of the laptop landscape, MacBook Neo would still be a good value. We’ll see what happens.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews.
  • According to recent reports, the coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” remarked recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”.

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” mentioned Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

According to recent reports, the coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”.

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks stated “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”.

She mentioned, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal complications and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks stated “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”.

According to recent reports, one job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the Fresh Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

It has been revealed that “We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she remarked. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”.

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”.

It has been revealed that “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they remarked, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

According to recent reports, she continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”.

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she remarked. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”.

Recent findings suggest that on the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” mentioned Brooks.

According to recent reports, but regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is vital,” mentioned the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that massive machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”.

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

Janeway thinks victory is possible, but Paris is dubious: he thinks they need more allies, and to push their Starfleet code of ethics like never before. Can you face down the Krenim without being wiped from the history books? You'll have to find out when Year of Hell is released for download on December 9.

In a months-long campaign against the Krenim, Voyager was battered and bruised, suffering heavy casualties as they assembled a ragtag coalition of the Krenim's foes. In the end, Captain Janeway sacrificed herself by crashing a near-derelict Voyager into Annorax's ship... and the resulting temporal shockwave restored everything back to where it had been before the events of the two-parter.

Sources indicate that the Year of Hell DLC will be available on December 9. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

It has been revealed that marvel Studios has a new Spider-Man for its multiverse releases, with Tom Holland having been recast as Peter Parker for certain projects, and it has worked out pretty seamlessly for the comic book giant despite the actor's popularity in the role. Spider-Man was always one of the world's most popular heroes, with every major Spider-Man movie to date being successful.

Industry observers note that that remarked, there is no denying that Holland's Spider-Man franchise has put the character on a latest shelf. After all, earlier this year, Spider-Man: Brand New Day became the 3rd highest-grossing movie of all time, earning over $2.5 billion worldwide, a number that will rise when its re-release starts playing in theaters on December 4. The Marvel movie's theatrical return will feature an Avengers: Doomsday scene.

Industry observers note that all this success comes down to audiences loving what Holland has brought to the table as Spider-Man and his MCU journey from a newcomer in the middle of a superhero civil war to a young, but experienced hero who carries a lot of trauma, pushing through the pain and inspiring others, such as Sadie Sink's Jean Grey and Jon Bernthal's Punisher. Holland's Spider-Man is an icon.

Sources indicate that as such, with Avengers: Secret Wars expected to reboot the MCU in some form, Holland is most likely to stay on as Spider-Man, even though other characters should be recast. Marvel is not insane to replace the one who is arguably its most popular hero. That said, the MCU's multiverse slate of projects has already recast Holland's Spider-Man, and I have to say that it worked out great for them.

Sources indicate that while Holland has starred in four Spider-Man movies and other MCU projects, the actor has never given life to Peter Parker on the small screen. Fans have been asking for Spidey to show up in Daredevil: Born Again for years, and even though several MCU actors have voiced their characters across Marvel Studios' animated projects, Holland did not return as the wall-crawler in them. All of this likely boils down to the fact that Sony owns Spider-Man's movie rights, while Marvel can do as it pleases with animation, and the gray areas in which Holland could play Spidey are probably too complicated to sort out.

According to recent reports, well, this contractual dilemma has led to Marvel recasting Spider-Man, with the same actor voicing Peter Parker in three animated TV shows on Disney+. Hudson Thames started his MCU multiverse journey as Spider-Man's voice in What If…?, with the actor returning for that show's zombie-themed spin-off, Marvel Zombies, as well as a Spider-Man series created by Marvel Studios, Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man. While one might say that Thames' Spidey is part of the multiverse, not directly connected to the MCU, which is correct, it is clear that he is essentially Holland's Spider-Man, but on TV and without contractual challenges.

Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man is pretty much an alternate universe that is close enough to the MCU, while also forging a new path for itself. In the animated Marvel series, Thames' Spider-Man is mentored by Colman Domingo's Norman Osborn, rather than Iron Man, and that event sets Peter up for an unpredictable chain of events, though the superhero Civil War and other MCU elements also play out in the series. Scorpion looks like Michael Mando, Charlie Cox voices Daredevil in the show, and above everything else, Peter Parker is, personality-wise, the same as Holland's version. Even Aunt May is pretty much the same.

Sources indicate that thames brings that same boyish charm and charisma, as well as the quip machine Holland made his version of Spider-Man, but also all the emotional depth the character needs. It is a masterclass in how to bring Spider-Man into animation with all of his core traits, while forging a newly introduced path for him in relation to the adventures Holland has in the MCU, be that through having Harry Osborn as his best friend, surviving the zombie apocalypse, or much more throughout those three animated shows in the MCU multiverse. Marvel Studios has left Spider-Man in good hands in all mediums.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].
  • “I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale.
  • Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.].

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”.

Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season.

It has been revealed that he’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

The finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke stated. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”.

It has been revealed that but Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”.

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

Sources indicate that “When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”.

Sources indicate that “That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke remarked. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”.

In a recent development, in Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke stated. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in Fresh York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”.

Industry observers note that “We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”.

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”.

According to recent reports, “The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke said. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”.

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”.

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other substantial finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

Recent findings suggest that “The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo said. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”.

In a recent development, “And that’s what I did. It has this bit of nostalgia. It also has this magic to it and this dreamlike quality to what he’s doing,” Harjo said. “The character is such an internal person that the only way you’re going to get those monologues is through a journal when he thinks it’s the privacy of himself and his journal. He’s expressing things that he wouldn’t normally express out loud.”.

In a recent development, “Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he stated, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”.

Sources indicate that throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

Industry observers note that “Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke mentioned. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”.

“But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”.

According to recent reports, one way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

Industry observers note that “The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke said. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”.

In a recent development, while another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo mentioned. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”.

Sources indicate that “Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”.

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be confirmed is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future ….

Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated problems coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication matter affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

Recent findings suggest that however, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith claims it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

It has been revealed that A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

According to recent reports, but that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

It has been revealed that aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

In a recent development, indieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the massive one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”.

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very promptly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

In a recent development, I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really significant challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

According to recent reports, but then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

In a recent development, he’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

It has been revealed that A couple of things really that had a really substantial impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone remarked to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

According to recent reports, you are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

Industry observers note that I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”.

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”.

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”.

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

According to recent reports, I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

According to recent reports, so, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

According to recent reports, yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

It has been revealed that obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s crucial to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

Industry observers note that I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

In a recent development, you are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a massive breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

In a recent development, we can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the tech giant even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start ….

It has been revealed that the science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the tech giant ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing plans for autonomous AI agents.

According to recent reports, we’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK.

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that growing up around performers, storytelling was always central to Emma's life. Add in a nerdy older brother who introduced her to Marvel at far too young an age, and her love for entertainment led her to pursue a Journalism degree at Indiana University, where she discovered her passion for entertainment reporting. She spent nearly one year in Los Angeles covering industry stories and fully immersing herself in the world of entertainment media.

Netflix's The Body is off to a promising start on the streaming charts.

Industry observers note that according to Nielsen's Top 10 Streaming Chart, the eight-part psychological thriller accumulated 498 million minutes viewed during the week of November 9–15, equivalent to 8.3 million hours. The series, which released all eight episodes on November 11, secured the No. 6 spot on Nielsen's Original Streaming Programs chart within its first five days of availability.

The Netflix series outperformed several other new streaming titles, including Hulu's The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County (461 million minutes) and Peacock's The Good Daughter (398 million minutes). Meanwhile, Prime Video's The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power topped the Originals chart with 866 million minutes following its season 3 premiere.

Created by Quinn Shephard, the writer-director behind the Emmy-nominated crime drama Under the Bridge, The Body follows a group of Catholic schoolgirls who begin experiencing prophetic visions after a dance-team initiation goes wrong, triggering mass hysteria throughout their town.

Recent findings suggest that the main characters of The Body are played by Kristina Bogic, Sara Boustany, Geena Meszaros, Nnamdi Asomugha, Shirley Chen, and High School Musical: The Musical: The Series star Sofia Wylie. The ensemble cast also includes The Traitors winner Gabby Windey.

The Body was the third most-watched Netflix series on Nielsen's Originals chart, behind Black Doves and Love Is Blind, while outperforming established titles such as The Great British Baking Show.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County.

Per Netflix, Shephard revealed that she drew inspiration from horror movies, coming-of-age stories, and psychological thrillers she loved growing up, including Carrie, Jennifer's Body, Heavenly Creatures, and Mean Girls. The series also marks a creative reunion between Shephard and Emmy nominee Riley Keough, who previously starred in and executive produced the true-crime drama Under the Bridge.

In addition to its streaming success, The Body has been well received by critics and audiences. According to Rotten Tomatoes, the series presently holds a Certified Fresh 84% critics' score from 32 reviews, alongside an even higher audience score of 95% from over 1,000 ratings.

In ScreenRant's review of The Body, Dani Kessel Odom praised the series' religious satire and campiness but criticized its inconsistent pacing and cliffhanger ending.

The Body isn't the only horror series finding success on Netflix. During the same measurement period, the acquired sci-fi horror series From topped Nielsen's overall streaming chart for the fourth consecutive week with approximately 1.55 billion minutes viewed. Since joining Netflix on October 19, the series has accumulated 6.92 billion viewing minutes.

Sources indicate that despite its strong reception from critics and audiences, Netflix has yet to officially renew The Body season 2, as of November 17. The thriller leaves several of its major storylines unresolved. However, showrunners Gina Gammell and Shephard already have ideas for a potential second season.

It has been revealed that while Netflix has a history of canceling supernatural teen dramas after just one season, including shows such as First Kill and I Am Not Okay with This, The Body's impressive streaming debut could bode well for its future. With The Body season 1 leaving so many unanswered questions, a renewal would give the creative team an opportunity to further explore the show's central mystery.

The Body is presently available to stream on Netflix.
