Nvidia today revealed that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Manufacturer. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”.

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

  • Sources indicate that given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

Recent findings suggest that A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

Sources indicate that given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Sources indicate that cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

According to recent reports, “All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino remarked in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”.

In a recent development, tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report indicates that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting newly introduced sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character states that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

Sources indicate that when you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

It has been revealed that the film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the Fresh Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

It has been revealed that if you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the aims to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV demonstrates, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

Industry observers note that the only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

In a recent development, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ah, the Academy Awards. Every year, cinephiles tune in for the big event as the Oscars honor the best of the best of the previous year in cinema. And like most viewers, opinions are not only present; everybody has one. While those opinions usually arrive the day nominations are officially revealed, they linger well beyond when the sealed envelope is opened, and the winner is revealed. In the almost century the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has handed out the gold statuette, a handful of decisions have left us baffled.

In a recent development, from brutal robberies to jaw-dropping shocks, when the Oscars botch it, we make our opinions loud and clear. There are certainly more than ten times that they’ve made the wrong decision; these ten are the absolute worst. Perhaps it was the fact that some of the greatest films of all time were beaten out, or the voters were too prejudiced to make a bold decision; these horrible wins meant deserving projects, performers, and creators lost. Though some individuals earned their award at another time, others are still waiting. While the biggest travesty in Academy Awards history is that Glenn Close doesn’t have a performance trophy, these other decisions continue to have us scratching our heads.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps this category had many people in shock the moment the nominations were announced because it meant that Eurovision Song Contest: Story of Fire Saga was an Oscar nominee. But the truth is, its nomination was well warranted. And it’s not just because I’m a die-hard Eurovision fanatic. Their entry, “Husavik (My Hometown),” is actually a remarkable track. Unfortunately, even with a stunning performance from Molly Sandén “live” on a boat in Iceland with an Icelandic child choir on Oscar night, it was still not enough to sway voters. Instead, the honor was given to “Fight for You” from Judas and the Black Messiah. The song authentically captured the late-1960s soul and funk sound of the film while speaking directly to contemporary themes of racial injustice.

Sources indicate that performed by H.E.R. with music by H.E.R. and Dernst Emile II, with lyrics by H.E.R. and Tiara Thomas, the song addresses racism, police brutality, and state repression, linking Hampton's story and COINTELPRO to modern racial justice movements. Its message aligned closely with broader racial justice conversations and H.E.R.'s recent Grammy Song of the Year win for "I Can't Breathe.” Though a great song, it had momentum to ride on. Though it changed drastically, as we’ll discuss later, the Academy voting trends often favor socially urgent anthems over comedic or parody films. For those familiar with the source material on which Eurovision Song Contest: Story of Fire Saga is based, “Husavik (My Hometown)” likely would have met a victory there. Nevertheless, at least the Will Ferrell comedy got an Oscar nod!

Industry observers note that margaret Thatcher is known for many things. From the infamous “The lady’s not for turning” to earning the nickname “Iron Lady,” she was ripe for a biopic. And if anyone was going to play her, one might think it would be a Brit. But the next best option is Meryl Streep. The legendary actress has a mantel full of Oscars and plenty of nominations to go with them. For her turn as Maggie Thatcher, it should have been simply another nomination as the win should have been given to Viola Davis for The Help. Streep was widely praised for capturing Thatcher's posture, voice, and steely resolve while finding the human vulnerability beneath the political figure. But it was by no means her strongest performance. In fact, a major factor in her victory was the headline: Streep’s third Oscar win ended a 29-year drought after 12 straight defeats.

According to recent reports, while Streep did earn the Golden Globe and BAFTA, a precursor to the Oscar win, the film itself wasn’t well received. Her victory may have stemmed from reverence. It gave voters a long-overdue milestone moment. Distributor Harvey Weinstein ran a heavy awards push for The Iron Lady, and at the time, it carried a lot of weight. Although Davis won the Screen Actors Guild Award and The Help was a box-office hit, the film lacked directing or writing nominations and also had running mate Octavia Spencer competing for acting recognition. Davis finally earned a victory on her third try for Best Supporting Actress for her performance as Rose in Fences.

Recent findings suggest that as will be a trend moving forward, Best Picture wins are quite a touchy topic. One of the most shocking results from the ‘90s was when Shakespeare in Love beat out the war masterpiece Saving Private Ryan. The romantic dramedy reimagines a young, cash-strapped William Shakespeare (Joseph Fiennes) overcoming severe writer's block when he falls passionately in love with Viola de Lesseps (Gwyneth Paltrow), a wealthy noblewoman who disguises herself as a man to audition for his upcoming play, inspiring him to write Romeo and Juliet. It sounds like a lovely film, but was it the best of the year? Once again, producer Harvey Weinstein and Miramax pushed the film with an aggressive, politically inspired campaign.

Sources indicate that shakespeare in Love led all films with 13 Oscar nominations, ahead of Saving Private Ryan’s 11, and won the Screen Actors Guild ensemble award. As was clear, voters favored the lighter, witty romance over a grueling war drama, while Steven Spielberg still took home Best Director for Saving Private Ryan. Timing was also a potential factor, as Shakespeare in Love opened in December 1998 and expanded into early 1999 right as voting began, whereas Saving Private Ryan came out in July 1998. Campaigners reportedly pushed the narrative that Saving Private Ryan peaked in its opening D-Day sequence and dragged afterward. With Spielberg reportedly refusing to engage in similar mudslinging or aggressive counter-campaigning, Shakespeare in Love benefited from winning a campaign war.

It has been revealed that life is like a box of chocolates. Forrest Gump remains one of the most iconic films of the '90s. It's no coincidence that it beat out an equally iconic '90s classic: Pulp Fiction. But one was a safe film, and the other was a daring cinematic risk. Directed by Robert Zemeckis, Forrest Gump stars Tom Hanks as the kind-hearted, slow-witted Alabama man as he recounts his extraordinary life while unknowingly influencing major moments in 20th-century American history and pining for his lifelong love, Jenny Curran (Robin Wright). Forrest Gump was a film that was rooted in nostalgia. And for that, it received extra love. With broad emotional appeal and a less polarizing concept, Forrest Gump stood in great contrast to Pulp Fiction, which featured graphic violence and non-traditional morality that clashed with the mainstream Oscar taste of the time.

Forrest Gump was a massive commercial hit with star power and established pedigree. Coming off his win for Philadelphia, Forrest Gump was a crowd-pleaser. It also, for the time, stood out for its technical innovation in which its invisible CGI seamlessly inserted the performers into archival footage, helping it sweep six Oscars overall. And if it won the minor awards, of course the big one was it as well. The clash between the two films highlighted a great divide between traditional sentimentality and '90s postmodernism. Pulp Fiction's risky storytelling was awarded as Quentin Tarantino won for Best Original Screenplay, but the gritty, non-linear crime story was ahead of its time. Tarantino has argued that the Golden Globes placing the film in the drama category over Musical or Comedy hurt its chances, as it established a specific serious tone for award season despite its dark humor. Nevertheless, when we examine the best films of the decade, Pulp Fiction and even the other big loser, The Shawshank Redemption, tend to be placed above Forrest Gump.

It has been revealed that academy voters have great reverence for industry legends, especially when they've built a steadfast career without a win. So, while Jamie Lee Curtis was arguably in the greatest film of the year, was she actually the best supporting actress in that film? Everything Everywhere All at Once remains one of the most triumphant stories of the 2020s. The daring multi-genre film defied the odds, rightly earning all of the praise it received. At the Oscars, it won seven of the 11 nominations it was up for, but the controversial win was when it beat itself. Curtis won for Best Supporting Actress playing IRS inspector Deidre Beaubeidre, blending comedy, action, and emotional weight, even when she sported a bob and hot dog hands. She defeated her co-star, Stephanie Hsu, and it likely came down to a mix of career-long goodwill, strategic campaigning, and late-season awards momentum.

According to recent reports, as an industry veteran, Curtis' win was a career win for her memorable, vanity-free performance. She was a scene-stealer in a character role compared to Hsu's double parts as Joy Wang and Jobu Tupaki. To some, Tsu was the emotional core and a co-lead. And, unfortunately, she would had no shot against Michelle Yeoh should she have been placed in that category. While Hsu has downplayed and dismissed any rivalry, sharing support and happiness for Curtis' win, many people believed that Hsu's loss undercut the importance of spotlighting Asian visibility that came with the film. Perhaps it came down to some unfortunate vote-splitting, or it was all about Curtis' grassroots championing of the film and her impactful off-the-cuff SAG Award acceptance speech, but Hsu was snubbed for an equally incredible performance.

For many of these entries, we're focusing on a one-on-one race. Except for this one. The King's Speech defeated so many incredible films that we're all still baffled. Let's discuss. In the Tom Hooper film, the story follows Britain's reluctant King George VI (Colin Firth) as he works with an unorthodox Australian speech therapist, Lionel Logue (Geoffrey Rush), to overcome a debilitating stammer before addressing his nation at the start of World War II. Biopics tend to do well at the Oscars. It was no different here. Yet it faced heavy hitters, including Black Swan, Inception, The Social Network, and True Grit. So, how was it victorious? The King's Speech combined broad crowd-pleasing appeal, acclaimed acting performances, typical Oscar-bait storytelling, and preferential treatment.

Many have pointed to The King's Speech's classic prestige as a natural fit for traditional voters. Especially during a ranked-choice voting system, which tends to reward films with broader backing rather than divisive favorites. Yet history has shown that its competitors are the films that truly stood the test of time. As an inspiring, emotionally accessible choice with strong above-the-line wins, it was not enough for the other films to overcome the hurdle. The Social Network emerged as its biggest competitor, having a strong early push, but lost out in crucial categories. Inception rightly achieved four technical Oscars, but its voters were not on board for the high-concept sci-fi thriller. Natalie Portman won for Black Swan, but when Clint Mansell's score was disqualified from Oscar consideration for relying heavily on Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, the film lost most of its momentum. And True Grit went 0-for-10. Needless to say, the 83rd Academy Awards was a doozy!

It's time to journey back to 1941 when one of the greatest films ever made, Citizen Kane, won the Academy Award for Best Picture. Scratch that. When it LOST the Academy Award for Best Picture. Mind-blowing! One of the biggest shockers in Oscar history came down to a preference for nostalgia, a beloved director, and a media mogul's fervent push to prevent a victory. Citizen Kane failed to win Best Picture, losing to How Green Was My Valley. Based on the book by Richard Llewellyn, the John Ford drama follows youngest son Huw Morgan (Roddy McDowall) as he looks back on his close-knit family's joys, labor struggles, and gradual dissolution in a turn-of-the-century South Wales coal-mining town. How Green Was My Valley was victorious for its combined prestige, studio craftsmanship, and emotional family drama with wartime appeal. Having come off of back-to-back Best Director wins, Ford set the industry standard. Orson Welles made a mark in a very different way.

Recent findings suggest that 25-year-old Welles, a relative newcomer to the industry, faced the ire of newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst, making voters wary of backing it. Hearst viewed Citizen Kane as a personal attack and used his newspapers to suppress coverage and hurt the film's box office. Welles was seen as a brash outsider disrupting studio norms, using themes of power and isolation to tell his story. His confidence ruffled feathers, resulting in the film's punishment. That remarked, Citizen Kane wasn't viewed as the masterpiece we see it as today. Following Pearl Harbor, How Green Was My Valley was the safer, more comforting option. This defeat remains one of the more peculiar decisions in Oscar history.

Sources indicate that the 2003 Academy Awards were quite controversial. The ceremony was well before cancel culture was the way of the world, so artistic merit outweighed personal conflict. So Roman Polanski's Best Director win for The Pianist wasn't because he didn't deserve it for his work, but the shock came from his troubled past. After widespread critical acclaim, Polanski earned the award through his deep personal connection to the material. Polanski survived the Holocaust as a child, which mirrored the survival themes within the source material. Between his passion behind the project and the belief that he had "paid his dues," Academy voters gave him the win. But he did not attend the ceremony because he remained a fugitive from the U.S. justice system since he pleaded guilty in 1978, ahead of sentencing, to unlawful sexual intercourse with a minor. His victory drew cheers and a standing ovation from parts of the audience, but it sparked a debate over separating an artist's personal crimes from their creative work.

In a recent development, had voters opted to give the win to another director, the options were Martin Scorsese for Gangs of Upcoming York and Rob Marshall for Chicago. It should be noted that the latter won for Best Picture. A major reason these two frontrunners lost was vote splitting. Scorsese won the Golden Globe while Marshall won the DGA Award. This opened the door for Polanski's upset. Despite Chicago's win, some long-time voters were not thrilled at the notion of honoring Marshall for his feature film debut. Gangs of New York also faced campaign backlash over Miramax's promotional tactics. While the overdue sentiment was overwhelmingly felt, Polanski's victory will forever be marred by controversy.

Surely you remember Art Carney's beloved performance as Harry Coombes in Harry and Tonto! Surely it's up to the same standard as Al Pacino as Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II and Jack Nicholson as J.J. "Jake" Gittes in Chinatown! Yeah, that's a bald-faced lie! And yet, it was Carney who won the Academy Award for Best Actor. Carney was recognized for his warm, understated performance as an evicted elderly widower traveling across America with his cat. Playing a 70-something at 55 with heavy makeup, Carney delivered a low-key, relatable portrayal full of heart and dignity. Yet extreme vote splitting between the Hollywood heavyweights kept the admired contenders off the Oscar stage. It should be noted that they also had to compete against Albert Finney in Murder on the Orient Express and Dustin Hoffman for Lenny, so needless to say, it was a tough year to be any of those men!

According to recent reports, against darker, more intense roles, Carney emerged as the safe, feel-good alternative. It was a win for a TV veteran who made a rare major massive-screen leading turn. But there may be more to the story. At least for Pacino. Some believe his earlier boycott of the 1972 ceremony and The Godfather Part II's major award sweep gave voters the leeway to deny him a trophy. The Godfather dynasty may have worked against Pacino, but why did Nicholson not emerge victorious? It may have come down to Chinatown's bleak, cynical ending, which went against Hollywood standards at the time. Though he may not have won for Chinatown, he did win a year later for One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.

Not going to lie, this one still stings. Surely Jack Nicholson read the wrong name, like the whole Moonlight-La La Land kerfuffle, right? Unfortunately, that was not the case, as Crash was victorious at the 2004 ceremony. Directed by Paul Haggis, Crash follows the interconnected lives of several strangers from diverse racial, cultural, and social backgrounds in post 9/11 Los Angeles whose paths unexpectedly collide over a volatile 36-hour period, forcing them to confront prejudice, bigotry, and urban disconnect. The film won thanks to strong support from its massive ensemble, an aggressive DVD screener campaign, and cultural pushback against its rival, Brokeback Mountain. Yes, you read that right. The gay cowboy film was too progressive for the time.

Sources indicate that lionsgate sent over 100,0000 screeners to SAG members and other voters. Because actors formed the largest branch of the Academy, Crash was at the forefront of voters' minds. After winning the SAG Award for Best Ensemble, the momentum shifted toward the film in the stretch toward the Oscars. Oprah Winfrey featured the ensemble on her show. Roger Ebert championed the film as the top movie of the year. But Academy Award voters had to reckon with the fact that Ang Lee's brilliant film may have caused some discomfort. Brokeback Mountain was groundbreaking not just for highlighting a gay romance, but also for being set against a lush Western backdrop and disregarding the genre's tropes. There's no denying Crash's cultural impact, as it was essentially a Haggis passion project, but Brokeback Mountain pushed boundaries by celebrating a same-sex romance and focusing on the hardships of a taboo relationship through the lens of identity. Brokeback Mountain didn't leave the ceremony empty-handed, winning three Oscars for Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Original Score, but the supposed anti-gay bias and its subversion of classic Western masculinity became a voter turn-off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:.

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season.

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

Recent findings suggest that no need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so promptly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

It has been revealed that then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves swiftly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

In a recent development, the opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

Sources indicate that the latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Industry observers note that outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

It has been revealed that how Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of significant, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

It has been revealed that so long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

In a recent development, either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover newly introduced sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

#144060. Netflix’s 2-Season R-Rated Fantasy Series Is A Masterclass In Worldbuilding

Netflix’s 2-Season R-Rated Fantasy Series Is A Masterclass In Worldbuilding

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years.
  • Worldbuilding is an essential part of any fantasy series, as a well-defined setting helps viewers understand a society's magical elements, supernatural creatures, and physical laws, allowing them to become immersed in the story.
  • Dorohedoro is what happens when the darker elements of fantasy storytelling are pushed to a whole fresh level, resulting in an extremely quirky and fascinating journey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vanessa Piña has been writing as a journalist for over two years. As a senior writer, she focuses on timely coverage of the latest anime releases and popular comic franchises.

Worldbuilding is an essential part of any fantasy series, as a well-defined setting helps viewers understand a society's magical elements, supernatural creatures, and physical laws, allowing them to become immersed in the story. Striking the right balance is, in itself, a difficult task, since although some entries in the genre offer a detailed exposition of their settings, few series manage to integrate their fantastical elements in an original way. However, one underrated Netflix series has one of streaming's most unconventional and twisted magic worlds.

Dorohedoro is what happens when the darker elements of fantasy storytelling are pushed to a whole fresh level, resulting in an extremely quirky and fascinating journey. Rated TV-MA on Netflix, which makes sense, given how explosively violent it is, Dorohedoro doesn’t use disturbing imagery merely for shock value; instead, its gore serves to illustrate the social structure and the internal logic of its universe.

Industry observers note that released in 2020 by MAPPA, the studio behind hit series such as Jujutsu Kaisen and Attack on Titan, Dorohedoro features one of the most distinctive worlds in anime, characterized by an industrial aesthetic and a chaotic society that can only be brought to the screen through animation. The series is based on the seinen manga by Q Hayashida, which is aimed at adult readers and widely considered a masterpiece within this demographic, making it an essential work for any fan of dark fantasy.

Scrolling through Netflix's catalog, it is easy to find fantasy series that focus on hard worldbuilding, which prioritizes establishing complex rules to explain their magical elements. In this regard, Dorohedoro is one of the few series that successfully employs soft worldbuilding by avoiding exhausting lore dumps and over-explaining its mechanics, instead throwing viewers in a disordered dystopian setting that aligns with the story's tone.

The series follows Caiman, a man whose head has been magically transformed into that of a lizard and lost his memory. Armed only with a human head, which mysteriously sits inside his mouth and serves as a means of identification, and accompanied by his friend Nikaido, Caiman is set to find the sorcerer who cursed him, seeking both revenge and the truth about his identity. That way, Dorohedoro creates a unique atmosphere where viewers are just as confused as Caiman, using each bit of information provided to gradually piece together how the world and the magic of the sorcerers function.

That remarked, what makes Dorohedoro truly brilliant is the stark contrast between its two settings: the Sorcerers' World and The Hole, the latter being the desolate place where Caiman and Nikaido reside and where sorcerers ruthlessly harm its inhabitants to practice magic. The result is a world that feels alive in every respect, from the dynamics between those who live in The Hole and the sorcerers to the characters' side jobs outside acting as sorcerer hunters and the creative ways the series illustrates the consequences of using magic, as seen in the annual event "The Night of the Living Dead.".

Beyond its world-building and the intriguing mystery surrounding Caiman’s true identity, the charm of Dorohedoro is that it's a rather touching series. Even with its body horror, brutal killings, and abundance of gore, the anime is heartwarming at its core, incorporating dark comedy and lighthearted moments of camaraderie, showing the small joys in life such as sharing a meal. This makes the 23 episodes of Dorohedoro, spread across two seasons, particularly easy to binge-watch.

Recent findings suggest that the best part is that Dorohedoro still has plenty of story left to tell. With the anime having adapted around 80 chapters, it has reached roughly the halfway point of the manga. Fortunately, Dorohedoro Season 3 has already been confirmed.

How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every visual element in animation helps tell the story.
  • According to recent reports, “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others.
  • And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

According to recent reports, “Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It.

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

Recent findings suggest that according to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”.

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”.

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

It has been revealed that both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn mentioned. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”.

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”.

According to recent reports, one key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

According to recent reports, “The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”.

In a recent development, but Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”.

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”.

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush mentioned. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”.

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

“Hexed” is now playing in theaters.

Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials.
  • All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….
  • It has been revealed that apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….

It has been revealed that apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The manufacturer has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the manufacturer hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

Industry observers note that after its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple noted it was 95% of the way there.

Industry observers note that the company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and Fresh Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Recent findings suggest that potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

In a recent development, back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the organization is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”.

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are right now powered by Google’s Gemini models.

Recent findings suggest that at the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report stated the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

Industry observers note that what happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the manufacturer moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”.

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the firm’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Sources indicate that do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

'Star Trek: Deep Space Nine’s Greatest Quote Still Hasn't Been Beaten

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that star Trek: Deep Space Nine is the black sheep of the Star Trek franchise, a truth that has divided opinions ever since its debut in 1993.
  • It has been revealed that the quote comes in the fourth episode of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's first season: "A Man Alone." Constable Odo (René Auberjonois), Deep Space Nine's security chief, is wary of the influx of characters boarding the station via the recently discovered wormhole.
  • That intense dislike doesn't bode well for Odo after Ibudan is found dead in one of Quark's (Armin Shimerman) holosuites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that star Trek: Deep Space Nine is the black sheep of the Star Trek franchise, a truth that has divided opinions ever since its debut in 1993. It eschews the utopian future that was Gene Roddenberry's vision, with its enlightenment, moral fortitude, and the wonder of exploration, summed up in the "to boldly go where no man has gone before" phrase from its iconic opening narration. In its place is a gritty, darker series that takes place on a stationary outpost, where the ideal is constantly tested by moral ambiguity, subterfuge, and conflict. Nowhere is that challenge more evident than in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's greatest quote, one made 33 years ago that began as a statement of belief in moral righteousness, only to become one of dark irony as the series progresses.

It has been revealed that the quote comes in the fourth episode of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine's first season: "A Man Alone." Constable Odo (René Auberjonois), Deep Space Nine's security chief, is wary of the influx of characters boarding the station via the recently discovered wormhole. He takes particular offense to one, Ibudan (Stephen James Carver), who had been a smuggler of goods to Bajorans during the Cardassian Occupation. The popular opinion is that Ibudan is a hero; only Odo doesn't share that opinion. He tells Commander Sisko (Avery Brooks), after getting into a fight with Ibudan, that Ibudan had, after a young girl's parents were unable to pay for his smuggled goods, callously let her die. Strike one, in Odo's mind, and strike two came when Ibudan killed a Cardassian officer.

That intense dislike doesn't bode well for Odo after Ibudan is found dead in one of Quark's (Armin Shimerman) holosuites. Odo is now the prime suspect, prompting Sisko to warn him that he is not to breach protocol or take the law into his own hands. Odo retorts with the series' greatest quote:.

According to recent reports, "Laws change, depending on who's making them — Cardassians one day, Federation the next. But, justice is justice.".

Sources indicate that in context, Deep Space Nine had only recently come under joint Federation-Bajoran administration following the extended, harsh occupation by the Cardassians. Odo's role, however, has not changed under the new regime: he was the enforcer of the law under the Cardassians, and now he is under the joint administration. As one would expect, the written laws under Cardassian rule were far more Draconian than those of Starfleet, so the idea of what is right is fluid, depending on who's in charge. Odo, by his very nature, sees justice as an absolute principle, a standard of morality that is true and right regardless of what the powers-that-be dictate. Or, as he so elegantly states it, "Justice is justice.".

History is littered with examples of government edicts that contradict what is morally right – look no further than Nazi Germany as a perfect example – so Odo is not wrong. But as the series progresses, Odo's strict adherence to order and fairness is challenged regularly, forcing him to see that his black-and-white thinking is more complicated in this gray environment. Order is only maintained by obeying the law, where justice often means breaking it: the pursuit of both is an exercise in futility.

And then things take a darkly ironic turn when Odo, a Changeling, discovers his origins in the Season 3 premiere two-parter, "The Search, Part I" and "The Search, Part II." That part of Odo that sees order as an absolute is, indeed, an innate part of his people, a fundamental principle they cling to. The part of Odo that seeks justice, however, is learned. Where Odo sees justice as an absolute, the Changelings see control as an absolute instead, and couldn't care less about justice. The quote now, then, takes on a tragic irony where, in his heritage, justice isn't justice: justice is control. And it's that learned justice that forces Odo to turn against the Changelings and return to Deep Space Nine.

According to recent reports, the quote doesn't just apply to Odo's arc, but to the series as a whole. Laws don't apply in the face of the need for survival or to do what is just. The best example comes from Captain Sisko in "In the Pale Moonlight." In his pursuit of the greater good, he lies and schemes in order to bring the Romulans into the Dominion War. That pursuit inadvertently brings about the assassination of a Romulan senator, leaving Sisko to have to rectify how his actions brought it about and accept it, a casualty in the chase for justice. It's these types of complex narratives that tie directly, or indirectly, into Odo's quote that make Star Trek: Deep Space Nine a fuller, more mature entry in the Star Trek franchise.

#144050. iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it introduced in 2017.
  • With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch.
  • I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it introduced in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the fresh GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

Industry observers note that as a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

Sources indicate that airPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

According to recent reports, apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods users a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

It has been revealed that in testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk demonstrated 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

It has been revealed that does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

Sources indicate that if I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

Recent findings suggest that airPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.
